meta.blurb: A white rabbit in a waistcoat hurries past, checking his watch, and bored Alice follows him down a hole. Below, cakes change her size, a cat grins and fades away, and a furious Queen wants heads to roll.
meta.bible: Alice: a curious, polite seven-year-old girl in a blue dress who falls asleep on a riverbank. Her sister reads on the bank and wakes her at the end. Dinah: Alice's pet cat. The White Rabbit: a nervous rabbit in a waistcoat with a pocket watch, always late, who works for the Duchess and the Queen. Bill the Lizard: the Rabbit's servant, kicked out of the chimney. The Mouse: frightened of cats. The Dodo, a Duck, a Lory and an Eaglet: animals in the pool who run the Caucus-race. The Caterpillar: a blue Caterpillar on a mushroom, smokes a long pipe, asks Who are you. The mushroom: one side makes Alice grow, the other makes her shrink. The Pigeon: thinks Alice is a serpent. The Duchess: bad-tempered at first, kind later, finds a moral in everything. The Cook: throws pots and pans, uses too much pepper. The Cheshire Cat: grins, appears and vanishes, says we are all mad here. The Mad Hatter, the March Hare and the Dormouse: the Mad Tea-Party, always six o'clock because they quarrelled with Time. The Queen of Hearts: furious, shouts Off with her head. The King of Hearts: mild, hushes her. The Knave of Hearts: accused of stealing the Queen's tarts. The Gryphon and the Mock Turtle: the Mock Turtle's lessons are Reeling, Writhing, Ambition, Distraction, Uglification and Derision. The Lobster Quadrille. Rule Forty-two. Rule One. Wonderland: a dream world under the ground. Places: the riverbank, the rabbit hole, the hall of doors, the pool of tears, the little garden door, the Rabbit's house, the wood, the Duchess's kitchen, the Queen's croquet-ground, the courtroom. Objects: a tiny golden key, a bottle marked Drink me, a cake marked Eat me, the Rabbit's white gloves and fan, flamingo mallets, hedgehog balls. Voice and tone: warm, playful, curious; dream logic, wit and gentle humour. Nothing is truly frightening, and the ending is a waking, happy one. More fixed names and things for the full-length version. Mary Ann: the housemaid the White Rabbit mistakes Alice for. Pat: the Rabbit's gardener, who says he is digging for apples. Father William: the poem Alice recites wrongly to the Caterpillar. Footman: the Fish-Footman and the Frog-Footman at the Duchess's door. Croquet: the Queen's game; Flamingo and Flamingos are the mallets, Hedgehog and Hedgehogs the balls, and soldiers bent double are the arches. Cheshire: the Duchess's cat is a Cheshire cat. Gardeners: Two, Five and Seven, card gardeners painting white roses red. The executioner: will not cut off a head without a body. Treacle: the Dormouse's story is about three sisters, Elsie, Lacie and Tillie, in a Treacle well; things that begin with an M are Mousetraps, the Moon, Memory and Muchness. Thimble: Alice's prize in the Caucus-race; Comfits are the sweets she gives out as prizes. Tortoise: what the pupils called their old master, because he taught us. Porpoise: no wise fish goes anywhere without one; the Whiting and the Snail are in the Lobster Quadrille song; Beautiful Soup is the Mock Turtle's song. Seaography and Drawling: lessons at the Mock Turtle's school. Tarts: the Queen's tarts, which the Knave is accused of stealing. Teacup: the Hatter's teacup. Jury: twelve creatures in a jury-box, with Slates and Bill's squeaking Pencil. Wig: the King wears one over his crown. Rule Forty-two: anyone more than a mile high must leave the court; Alice says that makes it Rule One. The Knave is made of cardboard and cannot swim. The ending: Alice wakes on the riverbank and her sister dreams of Wonderland.
chapters: The Oldest Rule in the Book

beats.scene: Alice sits bored on a sunny riverbank beside her sister, who is reading
beats.summary: Alice is bored on the riverbank while her sister reads a book without pictures.

beats.scene: Alice half asleep in the warm sun, thinking about making a daisy chain
beats.summary: The hot day makes Alice sleepy, and she wonders whether a daisy chain is worth the trouble.

beats.scene: A white rabbit with pink eyes hurries past Alice, muttering to himself
beats.summary: A White Rabbit runs by, muttering that he will be late.

beats.scene: The White Rabbit takes a pocket watch from his waistcoat and looks at it
beats.summary: The Rabbit looks at a watch from his waistcoat pocket, which amazes Alice.

beats.scene: Alice dives into a rabbit hole under a hedge, chasing the white rabbit
beats.summary: Alice chases the Rabbit and plunges into his burrow without thinking how to get out.

beats.scene: Alice falls through a deep dark well lined with cupboards and shelves
beats.summary: The burrow becomes a deep well, and Alice falls so slowly that she can look around.

beats.scene: Alice reaches for a jar marked orange marmalade from a passing shelf
beats.summary: Alice takes down an empty jar of marmalade and puts it in a cupboard as she falls.

beats.scene: Alice drifts downward in the dark, thinking of her cat Dinah
beats.summary: Still falling, Alice talks to herself about her cat Dinah and her saucer of milk.

beats.scene: Alice lands with a thump on a heap of dry leaves and sticks
beats.summary: Alice dozes off, wondering whether cats eat bats, and lands unhurt on a heap of leaves.

beats.scene: Alice runs along a dim passage toward the white rabbit far ahead
beats.summary: Alice jumps up and chases the Rabbit down a long passage.

beats.scene: Alice stands in a long low hall lit by lamps hanging from the roof
beats.summary: Alice turns the corner, loses the Rabbit, and finds herself in a long low hall lit by lamps.

beats.scene: Alice tries the handle of one locked door after another along the hall
beats.summary: Doors line the hall on every side, but they are all locked.

beats.scene: A little three-legged glass table holds a tiny golden key in the hall
beats.summary: Alice finds a glass table with a tiny golden key on it.

beats.scene: Alice lifts a low curtain to find a little door fifteen inches high
beats.summary: Behind a low curtain is a little door, and the golden key fits its lock.

beats.scene: Alice kneels and peeps through a small door at a bright garden
beats.summary: The door opens on a small passage and a view of a lovely garden.

beats.scene: Alice's head is stuck at the little door, and her shoulders will not follow
beats.summary: Alice cannot fit through the door and wishes she could shut up like a telescope.

beats.scene: Alice returns to the glass table and finds a small bottle labelled Drink me
beats.summary: Back at the table, Alice finds a bottle with a paper label that says Drink me.

beats.scene: Alice sips from the little bottle with a thoughtful face
beats.summary: Alice checks that the bottle is not marked poison, then tastes it and finishes it.

beats.scene: Alice, only ten inches tall, beams at the little door
beats.summary: Alice shrinks to ten inches tall and wonders whether she will vanish like a candle.

beats.scene: Tiny Alice cries beside the tall glass table, near a glass box with cake
beats.summary: Alice has forgotten the key, cannot climb the table, and finds a cake marked Eat me.

beats.scene: Alice stretches taller and taller like a telescope in the hall
beats.summary: Alice eats the cake and grows, so surprised that she forgets how to speak properly.

beats.scene: Alice looks down at her feet, now far below her in the hall
beats.summary: Her feet are so far away that she says goodbye to them and wonders who will dress them.

beats.scene: Alice writes a letter to her own feet, addressed to her right foot
beats.summary: Alice plans to send her feet new boots every Christmas and finds the idea absurd.

beats.scene: Giant Alice bumps her head on the roof of the hall, holding the key
beats.summary: Alice is now nine feet tall, bumps her head, and seizes the golden key.

beats.scene: Giant Alice lies on the floor, peeping at the garden with one eye
beats.summary: Alice lies down and looks at the garden with one eye, but cannot get in.

beats.scene: Alice weeps huge tears that spread across the floor of the hall
beats.summary: Alice scolds herself for crying, but her tears make a pool four inches deep.

beats.scene: The White Rabbit trots down the hall with white gloves and a large fan
beats.summary: The Rabbit returns, splendidly dressed, with white gloves and a fan, muttering about the Duchess.

beats.scene: Giant Alice speaks softly while the Rabbit drops gloves and runs away
beats.summary: Alice speaks to the Rabbit, and he is so frightened that he drops everything and flees.

beats.scene: Alice fans herself in the hot hall and slips on a white glove
beats.summary: Alice picks up the fan and one glove, and notices that she is shrinking.

beats.scene: Tiny Alice splashes into salt water at the foot of the little door
beats.summary: Alice drops the fan just in time, then slips and finds herself in salt water.

beats.scene: Tiny Alice treads water in a pool of salt water, looking around
beats.summary: Alice thinks she has fallen into the sea, then sees she is in her own pool of tears.

beats.scene: Alice swims toward a small mouse that has fallen into the pool
beats.summary: A small Mouse swims by, and Alice tries to speak to it, using her Latin lessons.

beats.scene: A frightened mouse leaps in the water as Alice speaks French
beats.summary: Alice speaks French, and the Mouse shivers with fear at the word cat.

beats.scene: Alice talks to a quivering mouse about her cat Dinah
beats.summary: Alice praises her cat Dinah, which only upsets the Mouse more.

beats.scene: The mouse swims away from Alice, bristling with fury at the talk of dogs
beats.summary: Alice mentions a terrier, the Mouse swims off, but Alice calls him back and he agrees to tell his story.

beats.scene: Birds and animals struggle in the pool and Alice leads them toward the shore
beats.summary: The pool fills with birds and animals, and Alice leads them all to the shore.

beats.scene: Wet birds and animals sit on the bank, quarrelling with Alice
beats.summary: The wet animals on the bank wonder how to get dry, and the Lory argues about age.

beats.scene: The Mouse stands on a stone, lecturing the wet circle of animals
beats.summary: The Mouse reads the driest history he knows, about William the Conqueror.

beats.scene: The Dodo stands among soggy animals, and the Eaglet hides a smile
beats.summary: Nobody dries, and the Dodo speaks in long words that nobody understands.

beats.scene: The Dodo draws a circle in the sand with his stick
beats.summary: The Dodo announces that a Caucus-race is the best way to get dry.

beats.scene: The Dodo marks a rough circle on the sand as animals line up
beats.summary: The Dodo marks out a circular course, and the animals stand along it.

beats.scene: Birds and animals run in all directions around the muddy circle
beats.summary: Everybody starts and stops when they like, until after half an hour they are dry.

beats.scene: The Dodo presses a finger to his forehead while the crowd pants around him
beats.summary: The Dodo declares that everybody has won and all must have prizes.

beats.scene: Alice hands round sweets from a box to a crowd of eager animals
beats.summary: Alice gives out comfits from her pocket as prizes, exactly one for each.

beats.scene: The Dodo solemnly presents a thimble to Alice as the others cheer
beats.summary: Alice is given her own thimble as a prize, and everyone cheers.

beats.scene: Birds choke and splutter over sweets while Alice pats their backs
beats.summary: The sweets cause noise and confusion, and then they all sit in a ring around the Mouse.

beats.scene: Alice looks puzzled at the Mouse's long curling tail
beats.summary: The Mouse sighs that his tale is long and sad, and Alice looks at his tail.

beats.scene: The Mouse glares angrily at Alice, who gazes at his long tail
beats.summary: Alice's mind wanders, and the Mouse scolds her for not listening.

beats.scene: The Mouse stalks away as animals flee when Alice mentions her cat
beats.summary: The Mouse walks off, and when Alice mentions Dinah, every creature hurries away.

beats.scene: Alice sits alone and sad beside the pool while a rabbit trots near
beats.summary: Alone and lonely, Alice cries, until the White Rabbit trots back, searching.

beats.scene: The White Rabbit searches the grass anxiously, muttering about the Duchess
beats.summary: The Rabbit searches for his gloves and fan, fearing the Duchess, while Alice sees the hall has gone.

beats.scene: The Rabbit points an urgent paw at Alice, who looks surprised
beats.summary: The Rabbit mistakes Alice for his housemaid Mary Ann and orders her to fetch his gloves.

beats.scene: Alice hurries to a neat little house with a brass plate reading W. Rabbit
beats.summary: Alice runs to a neat little house with the Rabbit's name on a brass plate and goes in.

beats.scene: Alice climbs stairs into a tidy bedroom with a table by the window
beats.summary: Alice thinks it is odd to run errands for a rabbit, and finds a fan and gloves.

beats.scene: Alice lifts a little uncorked bottle beside a looking-glass
beats.summary: Alice finds a bottle without a label and drinks, hoping to grow.

beats.scene: Alice's head presses against the ceiling of a small room as she stoops
beats.summary: She grows until her head hits the ceiling, and she regrets drinking so much.

beats.scene: Giant Alice, one arm out of the window and one foot in the chimney
beats.summary: Alice is stuck, with an arm out of the window and a foot up the chimney.

beats.scene: Stuck Alice lies on the floor thinking, her elbow against the door
beats.summary: Alice wonders whether she will ever grow up and why she can never get lessons done.

beats.scene: The Rabbit tries to open the door while Alice's elbow holds it shut
beats.summary: The Rabbit tries the door, then the window, and Alice snatches at him, and glass breaks.

beats.scene: The Rabbit shouts at his gardener Pat beside a broken cucumber frame
beats.summary: The Rabbit calls Pat, who says it is an arm in the window, and tells him to remove it.

beats.scene: Giant Alice snatches at the air again, with broken glass below the window
beats.summary: Alice makes a second snatch at the air, and more glass breaks outside.

beats.scene: A cartload of small animals carry ladders against the house
beats.summary: Outside, a crowd of voices fetches ladders and argues about who will do what.

beats.scene: The animals push Bill the Lizard toward the roof of the little house
beats.summary: The crowd decides that Bill the Lizard must go down the chimney, and Alice prepares to kick.

beats.scene: Bill the Lizard shoots up out of the chimney into the sky
beats.summary: Alice gives a sharp kick and Bill shoots up like a rocket.

beats.scene: A frightened lizard lies on the grass while others fuss over him
beats.summary: Bill is helped and tells what happened, and the Rabbit wants to burn the house down.

beats.scene: A shower of little pebbles turns into cakes on the floor
beats.summary: Alice threatens them with Dinah, and then pebbles begin turning into cakes.

beats.scene: Tiny Alice runs out of the house past guinea-pigs holding Bill
beats.summary: Alice eats a cake, shrinks, and runs out past the crowd and Bill.

beats.scene: Tiny Alice wanders among tall trees in a thick wood
beats.summary: Alice runs into the wood and makes a plan to grow back to her proper size.

beats.scene: A huge puppy peers down at tiny Alice with round eyes
beats.summary: A huge puppy looks down at tiny Alice, and she is afraid it will eat her.

beats.scene: Tiny Alice dodges a great thistle as the puppy chases a stick
beats.summary: Alice plays with the puppy and a stick, escapes, and rests beside a buttercup.

beats.scene: Tiny Alice looks up at a big mushroom among tall grass and flowers
beats.summary: Alice wonders how to grow again and finds a large mushroom nearly her own height.

beats.scene: Alice stands on tiptoe to look over a mushroom at a blue caterpillar
beats.summary: A blue Caterpillar sits on the mushroom, smoking a long pipe and ignoring her.

beats.scene: A blue caterpillar on a mushroom blows smoke and stares at Alice
beats.summary: The Caterpillar asks Alice who she is, and she says she hardly knows.

beats.scene: Alice and the Caterpillar face each other across the mushroom
beats.summary: Alice cannot explain herself, and the Caterpillar does not understand her troubles.

beats.scene: The Caterpillar rises up as Alice turns crossly away
beats.summary: Alice speaks of butterflies, quarrels with the Caterpillar and turns to leave.

beats.scene: The Caterpillar beckons Alice back with a curl of pipe smoke
beats.summary: The Caterpillar calls her back and asks her to recite a poem.

beats.scene: Alice stands with folded hands, reciting a verse to the Caterpillar
beats.summary: Alice recites Father William, but all the words come out wrong.

beats.scene: The Caterpillar lowers his pipe and glares at small Alice
beats.summary: The Caterpillar asks what size Alice wants to be, and she says three inches is too small.

beats.scene: The Caterpillar crawls off the mushroom into the long grass
beats.summary: The Caterpillar yawns, leaves the mushroom, and tells her one side makes her taller and one side shorter.

beats.scene: Alice stretches both arms round a round mushroom, breaking off two pieces
beats.summary: Alice puzzles over which side is which, and breaks off a piece from each edge.

beats.scene: Alice's chin presses against her feet as she holds a bit of mushroom
beats.summary: Alice nibbles the right-hand piece, shrinks so fast that her chin hits her foot, then eats the other piece.

beats.scene: Alice's long neck rises like a stalk above a sea of green leaves
beats.summary: Her head is free, but her shoulders are gone, and her neck rises above a sea of leaves.

beats.scene: Alice bends her long neck among the tree tops as a pigeon attacks
beats.summary: She bends her neck like a snake, and finds the leaves are tree tops, and a pigeon flies at her.

beats.scene: An angry pigeon flaps her wings in Alice's face
beats.summary: The Pigeon screams that Alice is a serpent and complains about serpents everywhere.

beats.scene: A pigeon sits on eggs in a tall tree, glaring at Alice
beats.summary: The Pigeon explains that she has not slept for three weeks because she is guarding her eggs.

beats.scene: Alice with her long neck argues with a sulky pigeon on her nest
beats.summary: Alice says she is a little girl, but the Pigeon thinks anyone who eats eggs is a serpent.

beats.scene: Alice kneels among tall trees, nibbling mushroom to change her size
beats.summary: Alice nibbles each piece of mushroom until she is back to her usual height.

beats.scene: Alice stands in a clearing before a small house about four feet high
beats.summary: Alice finds a little house in a clearing and nibbles until she is nine inches tall.

beats.scene: A fish-faced footman runs from the wood and knocks at a door
beats.summary: A Fish-Footman arrives with a large letter and knocks at the door, which is opened by a Frog-Footman.

beats.scene: Two footmen bow to each other, their powdered hair tangled together
beats.summary: The footmen deliver an invitation from the Queen to the Duchess, bow, and tangle their curls.

beats.scene: Alice knocks at a door while a footman stares at the sky
beats.summary: Alice knocks, but the Footman says there is no use, because of the noise inside.

beats.scene: A plate flies out of the open door past the footman's nose
beats.summary: The Footman ignores her question, and a plate flies out of the door and breaks on a tree.

beats.scene: The Footman whistles on the grass as Alice opens the door
beats.summary: The Footman answers every question with another question, and Alice goes in by herself.

beats.scene: A smoky kitchen where a duchess sits on a stool nursing a baby
beats.summary: The kitchen is full of smoke and pepper, and the Duchess, her baby and Alice all sneeze.

beats.scene: A big cat grins by the fire as the Duchess scolds
beats.summary: The cat is a Cheshire cat, which grins, and the Duchess is rude to Alice.

beats.scene: The cook throws pots and pans at the Duchess and the baby
beats.summary: The Cook flings pans and plates at the Duchess, and Alice cries out to mind the baby's nose.

beats.scene: The Duchess grumbles at Alice and sings a rough lullaby to the baby
beats.summary: The Duchess says the world would go faster if everyone minded their own business, and sings roughly to the baby.

beats.scene: The Duchess flings her baby at Alice and hurries out of the kitchen
beats.summary: The Duchess throws the baby to Alice and leaves for the Queen's croquet.

beats.scene: Alice carries a snorting baby out of the house into the fresh air
beats.summary: Alice carries the baby outside, afraid the Cook will hurt it, and it grunts.

beats.scene: A small pig trots away into the wood while Alice watches
beats.summary: The baby turns into a pig, and Alice lets it trot away.

beats.scene: The Cheshire Cat sits grinning on a tree branch above Alice
beats.summary: Alice sees the Cheshire Cat grinning on a branch and thinks it should be treated with respect.

beats.scene: Alice looks up at the grinning cat and asks for directions
beats.summary: Alice politely asks the Cat which way she ought to go.

beats.scene: The Cheshire Cat lounges on a branch as Alice stands puzzled below
beats.summary: The Cat says it depends where she wants to go, and she will get somewhere if she walks long enough.

beats.scene: The Cat waves one paw to the left and the other to the right
beats.summary: The Cat says a Hatter lives one way and a March Hare the other, and both are mad.

beats.scene: Alice frowns up at the Cat, who grins widely among the leaves
beats.summary: The Cat says that everyone here is mad, including Alice, or she would not have come.

beats.scene: The Cat grins as its tail swishes on the branch
beats.summary: The Cat argues that it is mad because it growls when pleased and wags its tail when angry.

beats.scene: The Cat vanishes and reappears on the branch as Alice looks on
beats.summary: The Cat asks if she will play croquet with the Queen, asks about the baby, and vanishes.

beats.scene: The Cat's grin hangs alone in the air above the branch
beats.summary: The Cat asks whether she said pig or fig and vanishes slowly, leaving only its grin.

beats.scene: Alice walks toward a house with ear-shaped chimneys and a roof of fur
beats.summary: Alice walks on to the March Hare's house, which has chimneys like ears and a roof of fur.

beats.scene: Alice, two feet tall, stands before the house nervously
beats.summary: Alice nibbles the mushroom until she is two feet tall and approaches nervously.

beats.scene: A long table under a tree where the Hatter and Hare drink tea
beats.summary: A table is set under a tree, where the March Hare and the Hatter drink tea with a sleeping Dormouse between them.

beats.scene: Alice sits in a large armchair at the end of a crowded table
beats.summary: The Hare and Hatter cry no room, but Alice sits down at the big table anyway.

beats.scene: The March Hare pours tea for a cross-looking Alice at the table
beats.summary: The Hare offers wine that does not exist, and Alice and the Hare trade rude remarks.

beats.scene: The Hatter stares at Alice, with a teacup in one hand
beats.summary: The Hatter says her hair needs cutting and asks why a raven is like a writing-desk.

beats.scene: The Hatter, the Hare and the Dormouse argue with Alice over tea
beats.summary: Alice tries to guess the riddle, and they argue that saying and meaning are not the same.

beats.scene: The Hatter shakes a pocket watch and the Hare dips it in tea
beats.summary: The Hatter checks the date on his watch and blames the butter for the broken works.

beats.scene: Alice peers over the Hatter's shoulder at his strange watch
beats.summary: Alice notes that his watch tells the date, not the time, and the Hatter has no answer to the riddle.

beats.scene: Alice sighs wearily while the Hatter shrugs over the teacups
beats.summary: Alice gives up the riddle and says they waste time, and the Hatter says that Time is a person.

beats.scene: The Hatter tosses his head as Alice talks of beating time
beats.summary: Alice says she beats time in music, and the Hatter says that Time will not stand beating.

beats.scene: The Hatter sings at the Queen's concert while the Queen glares
beats.summary: The Hatter tells how he quarrelled with Time at the Queen's concert, so it is always six o'clock.

beats.scene: The Hatter moves a dirty cup round a table scattered with teapots
beats.summary: The tea party keeps moving round the table, and the March Hare asks for a story instead.

beats.scene: The Hatter and Hare pinch a sleepy Dormouse awake at the table
beats.summary: The Dormouse wakes up and begins a story about three sisters who lived in a well.

beats.scene: Alice frowns as the Dormouse sits half asleep beside a teapot
beats.summary: The sisters lived on treacle and were ill, and Alice is told to take more tea.

beats.scene: The Hatter and Hare sit by a teapot, as the Dormouse speaks
beats.summary: The Dormouse says it was a treacle well, and the sisters were learning to draw treacle.

beats.scene: The Hatter shuffles to a new seat as the Hare spills a milk jug
beats.summary: Everyone moves one place round the table, and Alice gets the Hare's milky plate.

beats.scene: Alice asks a puzzled question while the Dormouse yawns and rubs its eyes
beats.summary: Alice asks where the treacle was drawn from, and the answer is from the well.

beats.scene: The sleepy Dormouse lists drawings that begin with the letter M
beats.summary: The Dormouse says the sisters drew things beginning with M, like mousetraps and muchness.

beats.scene: Alice walks off in disgust as the others stuff the Dormouse into a teapot
beats.summary: Alice leaves the tea-party, calling it the stupidest she has ever seen.

beats.scene: Alice finds a small door in a big tree trunk in the wood
beats.summary: Alice finds a door in a tree and goes through it into the hall again.

beats.scene: Alice kneels at the little door in the hall with the key and mushroom
beats.summary: Alice uses the key and a piece of mushroom to step into the garden at last.

beats.scene: Three card gardeners paint white roses red under a rose tree
beats.summary: In the garden, three gardeners painting white roses red quarrel with one another.

beats.scene: The three gardeners throw themselves flat on their faces
beats.summary: The gardeners explain that they planted white roses by mistake, and then the Queen's arrival makes them lie flat.

beats.scene: A procession of soldiers, courtiers, royal children and guests walks through the garden
beats.summary: A grand procession of soldiers, courtiers and royal children arrives, led by the White Rabbit and then the King and Queen.

beats.scene: The Queen of Hearts glares at Alice as the procession halts
beats.summary: The Queen asks who Alice is, and Alice reminds herself that they are only a pack of cards.

beats.scene: The Queen points at the gardeners while the King touches her arm
beats.summary: Alice boldly tells the Queen it is no business of hers, and the King begs the Queen to remember she is a child.

beats.scene: The Queen inspects the roses while three soldiers raise their spears
beats.summary: The Queen sentences the gardeners to lose their heads, and Alice hides them in a flower-pot.

beats.scene: Alice joins the procession as the Queen shouts across the garden
beats.summary: The Queen asks if Alice can play croquet, and Alice joins the procession.

beats.scene: The White Rabbit whispers anxiously to Alice as they walk
beats.summary: The White Rabbit whispers to Alice that the Duchess is under sentence of execution.

beats.scene: The Rabbit whispers in Alice's ear while she laughs in surprise
beats.summary: Alice laughs when she learns that the Duchess boxed the Queen's ears.

beats.scene: Players run in all directions across the garden as the Queen shouts
beats.summary: The Queen shouts at everyone to go to their places, and the players tumble about until the game begins.

beats.scene: A croquet-ground of ridges and furrows with live hedgehogs and flamingos
beats.summary: The croquet-ground is all ridges and furrows, with hedgehogs for balls, flamingos for mallets and soldiers for arches.

beats.scene: Alice struggles to hold a flamingo that twists its neck round
beats.summary: Alice cannot manage her flamingo, which looks up at her, while her hedgehog crawls away.

beats.scene: The angry Queen stamps across the garden while players squabble over hedgehogs
beats.summary: Everyone plays at once and quarrels, and the Queen shouts Off with his head every minute.

beats.scene: A grin and then a cat's head appear in the air beside Alice
beats.summary: Alice sees a grin in the air and the Cheshire Cat's head appears, so she has someone to talk to.

beats.scene: The Cat's head floats near Alice, who complains about the game
beats.summary: Alice complains that the game is unfair, and the Cat asks how she likes the Queen.

beats.scene: The King peers at the Cat's floating head while Alice introduces it
beats.summary: The King dislikes the look of the Cat and demands that it be removed.

beats.scene: The King hurries away while the Queen shouts across the garden
beats.summary: The Queen says to cut off the Cat's head, and the King goes to fetch the executioner.

beats.scene: Two hedgehogs fight while Alice chases a flamingo up the garden
beats.summary: Alice goes to find her hedgehog, which is fighting another hedgehog, and her flamingo has flown off.

beats.scene: The executioner, the King and the Queen argue around the Cat's floating head
beats.summary: A crowd gathers around the Cat's head, and the executioner, King and Queen argue about it.

beats.scene: The Cat's head fades into nothing as the King searches the air
beats.summary: Alice says the Cat belongs to the Duchess, so the Queen sends for her, and the Cat's head fades away.

beats.scene: The Duchess links arms with Alice as they stroll across the garden
beats.summary: The Duchess returns, friendly now, and Alice decides pepper makes people bad-tempered.

beats.scene: The Duchess rests her sharp chin on Alice's shoulder
beats.summary: The Duchess says everything has a moral and leans her sharp chin on Alice's shoulder.

beats.scene: Alice and the Duchess walk past a flamingo with its beak raised
beats.summary: The Duchess discusses flamingos and mustard, and finds a moral for each.

beats.scene: The Queen stands frowning with folded arms before Alice and the Duchess
beats.summary: The Duchess talks of more morals until the Queen appears, scowling like a storm.

beats.scene: Soldiers lead players away as the Queen shouts across the empty croquet-ground
beats.summary: The Queen frightens the Duchess away, and soon every player but Alice and the King is a prisoner.

beats.scene: A sleeping Gryphon lies in the sun as the Queen speaks to Alice
beats.summary: The Queen asks if Alice has seen the Mock Turtle and sends her with a sleeping Gryphon.

beats.scene: The Gryphon chuckles beside Alice as a Mock Turtle sobs on a rock
beats.summary: The Gryphon laughs that it is all the Queen's fancy, and they find the sad Mock Turtle.

beats.scene: A Mock Turtle sits on a rock, wiping his eyes with a flipper
beats.summary: The Mock Turtle sighs that he was once a real Turtle, and then sobs for a long time.

beats.scene: The Mock Turtle describes his school under the sea to Alice
beats.summary: The Mock Turtle says that he went to school in the sea with an old Tortoise as master.

beats.scene: The Mock Turtle counts lessons on his flippers while Alice listens
beats.summary: The Mock Turtle lists his lessons, including Reeling, Writhing and four kinds of Arithmetic.

beats.scene: The Gryphon raises both claws in surprise at Alice on the beach
beats.summary: Alice has never heard of uglifying, and the Mock Turtle lists more odd school subjects.

beats.scene: The Mock Turtle counts days on his flippers beside the Gryphon
beats.summary: The days of lessons get shorter, which is why they are called lessons.

beats.scene: The Mock Turtle sobs while the Gryphon pats his back on the beach
beats.summary: The Mock Turtle weeps, then asks if Alice has ever seen a Lobster Quadrille.

beats.scene: The Gryphon and Mock Turtle leap about in the sand, explaining the dance
beats.summary: The Gryphon and Mock Turtle explain the figures of the Lobster Quadrille.

beats.scene: The Mock Turtle and Gryphon dance around Alice, treading on her toes
beats.summary: They dance slowly around Alice while the Mock Turtle sings about a whiting and a snail.

beats.scene: The Mock Turtle yawns and shuts his eyes beside Alice on the beach
beats.summary: Alice describes whitings, and the Gryphon explains why they hold their tails in their mouths.

beats.scene: The Gryphon looks solemnly at Alice's shoes on the sand
beats.summary: The Gryphon explains that whitings polish boots and shoes under the sea.

beats.scene: The Mock Turtle shakes his head over a porpoise and Alice's adventures
beats.summary: The Mock Turtle says no fish goes anywhere without a porpoise, and the Gryphon asks for Alice's adventures.

beats.scene: Alice stands up straight to recite while the two creatures listen
beats.summary: Alice tells her adventures, and then she is made to recite a poem, which comes out wrong.

beats.scene: The Gryphon pulls Alice by the hand as the Mock Turtle sings far behind
beats.summary: The Mock Turtle begins a song about soup, but a cry that the trial is beginning interrupts, and the Gryphon runs off with Alice.

beats.scene: King and Queen of Hearts on thrones before a crowd, a chained Knave
beats.summary: Alice arrives at a court where the King and Queen sit on thrones and the Knave of Hearts stands in chains.

beats.scene: Twelve creatures write on slates in a jury-box beside the judge's throne
beats.summary: The King is the judge, and twelve creatures of different kinds are the jury.

beats.scene: A small lizard scratches with a squeaking pencil in the jury-box
beats.summary: Alice takes away the squeaking pencil of Bill the Lizard, and the jury is puzzled.

beats.scene: The White Rabbit blows a trumpet and unrolls a long scroll
beats.summary: The Rabbit reads out that the Knave of Hearts stole the Queen's tarts.

beats.scene: The Hatter holds a teacup and some bread-and-butter in the witness box
beats.summary: The Hatter, the first witness, arrives with his teacup and bread and butter.

beats.scene: The Hatter squirms in the witness box, wearing a tall hat
beats.summary: The King tells the Hatter to take off his hat, but he says it is not his, and he sells hats.

beats.scene: The Queen stares at the trembling Hatter through a pair of spectacles
beats.summary: The Queen stares at the Hatter, who trembles so much that he bites out of his teacup.

beats.scene: The Hatter mixes up his dates while the Dormouse grumbles beside Alice
beats.summary: The Hatter gives muddled evidence about his tea and a twinkle, while Alice starts to grow.

beats.scene: The Hatter runs out of court as a cook with a pepper-box enters
beats.summary: The Hatter is told to go and runs off, and the Cook enters with a pepper-box.

beats.scene: Giant Alice jumps up and overturns the jury-box with her skirt
beats.summary: Alice is called as the next witness, jumps up and overturns the jury-box.

beats.scene: Giant Alice kneels in the courtroom, gathering fallen jurors from the floor
beats.summary: Alice apologises and hurries to put the tumbled jurors back in their box.

beats.scene: A lizard sits upside down in the jury-box until Alice turns him upright
beats.summary: The King insists that every juror be in place, and Alice finds the Lizard upside down and puts him right.

beats.scene: The King peers sternly at Alice from his throne in the courtroom
beats.summary: The King asks what Alice knows about the matter, and she says nothing.

beats.scene: The White Rabbit whispers in the King's ear as jurors scribble
beats.summary: The Rabbit says that the King means unimportant, and the King mutters important and unimportant to himself.

beats.scene: Giant Alice stands in the court as the King reads from a little book
beats.summary: The King reads Rule Forty-two, that anyone over a mile high must leave, and says Alice must go.

beats.scene: Alice argues with the King, who turns pale and shuts his book
beats.summary: Alice says that the rule is new and calls it Rule One, so the King turns pale.

beats.scene: The White Rabbit holds up a paper as the Knave stands in chains
beats.summary: The Rabbit brings a paper that looks like a letter, but the Knave says he did not write it.

beats.scene: The King points at the Knave while the Queen nods
beats.summary: The King says that the letter shows the Knave meant mischief, and Alice says that proves nothing.

beats.scene: The White Rabbit unrolls a paper and reads verses to a silent court
beats.summary: The Rabbit reads a set of muddled verses, and Alice says there is not an atom of meaning in them.

beats.scene: The King spreads the verses on his knee and squints at the Knave
beats.summary: The King finds some meaning in the verses and decides that the Knave cannot swim.

beats.scene: The King points triumphantly at a dish of tarts as the Queen interrupts
beats.summary: The King sees the tarts in the verses and claims it is the best evidence yet, but the Queen demands the sentence first.

beats.scene: Giant Alice faces the purple-faced Queen across the crowded courtroom
beats.summary: Alice calls this nonsense, and the Queen orders her head off, but nobody moves.

beats.scene: Giant Alice stands tall over the courtroom as the cards rise up
beats.summary: Alice, now full size, says that they are nothing but a pack of cards.

beats.scene: A whole pack of cards flies into the air and falls down on Alice
beats.summary: The whole pack of cards flies up and falls on Alice, who screams and tries to beat them off.

beats.scene: Alice wakes on the riverbank as her sister brushes leaves from her face
beats.summary: Alice finds herself on the riverbank, with her head in her sister's lap.

beats.scene: Alice sits up on the bank, telling her sister the dream
beats.summary: Alice's sister wakes her, and Alice tells her all about her strange dream.

beats.scene: Alice's sister kisses her forehead on the sunny riverbank
beats.summary: Her sister kisses her, says it was a curious dream and sends her in to tea.

beats.scene: Alice runs across the field toward home in the late afternoon
beats.summary: Alice runs off to tea, thinking what a wonderful dream she has had.

beats.scene: Alice's sister sits dreaming on the bank while the sun sets
beats.summary: Alice's sister sits on the bank and dreams of Wonderland, hearing its voices and noises.

beats.scene: A grown-up Alice tells stories to a ring of eager children by a fire
beats.summary: Her sister imagines Alice grown up, telling the dream to children and remembering her happy summer days.

A1A2: Alice sits on the river bank with her sister, and she is bored.
The sun is hot, and Alice feels sleepy and thinks about picking flowers.
A White Rabbit with pink eyes runs past her and says, “I will be late.”
The Rabbit takes a watch out of his pocket and looks at it.
Alice runs after him and jumps into the big hole under the hedge.
The hole is deep, and Alice falls slowly past many shelves and cupboards.
She takes a jar from a shelf, but there is nothing in it.
Alice thinks about her cat Dinah and hopes someone gives her some milk.
Alice feels sleepy, and then she lands on a pile of dry leaves.
She is not hurt, and she jumps up and runs after the Rabbit.
Alice turns a corner, but the Rabbit is gone, and she is in a long hall.
The hall has doors on every side, but Alice finds that they are all locked.
In the middle of the hall, there is a glass table with a tiny golden key.
Behind a curtain, Alice finds a little door, and the golden key opens it.
Through the little door, Alice can see a beautiful garden full of flowers.
But her head is too big for the door, and she is sad.
Back at the table, Alice finds a small bottle with the words “Drink me.”
The bottle does not say poison, so Alice drinks it, and it tastes very good.
Suddenly Alice is only ten inches tall, and she is very happy.
But she forgets the key, cannot reach the table, and sits down and cries.
Alice eats the cake and grows very tall, and she says, “Curiouser and curiouser!”
Her feet are now far away, and she says goodbye to them.
She thinks, “Who will put on my shoes and socks now?”
Alice is nine feet tall now, and her head hits the roof.
She lies on the floor and looks at the garden with one eye.
Alice is sad, and she cries until a pool of tears is on the floor.
The Rabbit comes back with white gloves and a fan, and he is very worried.
Alice speaks to him, and he drops the gloves and fan and runs away.
Alice picks up the fan and a glove, and she feels very hot.
She drops the fan, and then she falls into water that is salty.
Alice falls into salty water and thinks she is in the sea.
Then she sees it is her own pool of tears, and a mouse swims by.
Alice speaks French to the Mouse, and he shakes with fear.
Alice says that her cat Dinah is nice, but the Mouse is not happy.
The Mouse swims away, but Alice calls him back, and he says yes.
Many birds and animals are in the water, and Alice takes them to land.
They are all wet, and they argue about how to get dry.
The Mouse tells them a dull story about William the Conqueror to dry them.
Nobody is dry, and the Dodo uses big words that nobody knows.
The Dodo says that a Caucus-race is the best way to get dry.
The Dodo draws a big circle, and the animals stand along it.
They run when they like and stop when they like, and soon they are dry.
The Dodo thinks for a long time, then says, “Everybody has won.”
Alice has sweets in her pocket, and she gives one to each animal.
The animals give Alice a thimble as her prize, and they all cheer.
They eat the sweets with a lot of noise, and then they sit down.
The Mouse says his story is long and sad, and Alice looks at his tail.
Alice does not listen, and the Mouse is angry with her.
The Mouse walks away, and when Alice says “Dinah,” all the animals run off.
Alone, Alice cries, and then she hears the Rabbit coming back.
The Rabbit looks for his gloves and fan and is very afraid of the Duchess.
He sees Alice and says, “Mary Ann, go home and get my gloves.”
Alice runs to a little house with the Rabbit's name on the door.
She goes upstairs and finds a fan and some white gloves on a table.
Next to the mirror is a little bottle, and Alice drinks from it.
She grows and grows until her head touches the ceiling.
She cannot get out, so she puts one arm out of the window.
Alice thinks about growing up, and she sits very still and feels sad.
The Rabbit cannot open the door, so he goes to the window.
Alice puts out her hand, and the Rabbit falls, and glass breaks.
Alice makes another snatch, and more glass breaks outside the window.
Outside, many animals bring ladders and argue about what to do.
They say that Bill the Lizard must go down the chimney.
Alice kicks hard, and Bill flies up into the sky.
They help Bill, and the Rabbit says, “We must burn the house down.”
Alice shouts about Dinah, and then stones fall in and turn into cakes.
Alice eats a cake, becomes small, and runs out of the house.
She runs into a thick wood and thinks about how to get big again.
A huge puppy looks down at her, and she is afraid.
She plays a game with the puppy, runs away, and rests by a flower.
Alice must grow big again, and she sees a large mushroom.
She looks over the top and sees a blue Caterpillar with a long pipe.
The Caterpillar asks who Alice is, and she says she hardly knows.
Alice says she is not herself, and the Caterpillar does not understand.
Alice talks about butterflies, then she gets angry and turns to go.
The Caterpillar calls her back and tells her to say a poem.
Alice says the poem, but the words come out all wrong.
The Caterpillar asks what size she wants, and Alice says three inches is too small.
The Caterpillar goes into the grass and says one side makes her taller.
Alice does not know which side is which, so she breaks off two pieces.
Alice eats a little of the mushroom, and her chin hits her foot.
Then she eats the other piece, and her neck grows very long.
She bends her neck like a snake, and a Pigeon flies at her face.
The Pigeon screams that Alice is a serpent, because of her long neck.
The Pigeon has not slept for three weeks because she watches her eggs.
Alice says she is a girl, but the Pigeon does not believe her.
Alice eats small bits of mushroom until she is her right size again.
She finds a little house and eats a bit more, so she can go near.
A footman with a fish's face runs up and knocks at the door.
The Frog-Footman opens the door, and they bow so low that their curls get stuck.
Alice knocks on the door, but the Footman says it is no use.
A plate flies out of the door and breaks on a tree.
The Footman will not help, so Alice opens the door and goes in.
The kitchen is full of smoke, and the pepper hurts Alice's nose.
A big cat sits and grins, and the Duchess is rude to Alice.
The Cook throws pans at the Duchess and the baby, and Alice is afraid.
The Duchess sings a rough song to the baby and shakes it.
The Duchess throws the baby to Alice and runs out to play croquet.
Alice carries the baby outside, and it makes a noise like a pig.
The baby turns into a pig, and Alice lets it walk away.
Alice sees the Cheshire Cat on a tree, and it is grinning.
The Cat has long claws, so Alice asks very politely which way to go.
The Cat says it depends where she wants to go.
The Cat says a Hatter lives that way and a March Hare lives that way.
The Cat says everyone here is mad, and Alice must be mad too.
The Cat says it is mad, because it acts the opposite of a dog.
The Cat asks about the baby, and Alice says it turned into a pig.
The Cat disappears slowly and leaves only its grin in the air.
Alice walks to the March Hare's house, and it has a roof of fur.
Alice eats a little more mushroom and feels nervous about going closer.
Under a tree, the Hatter and the March Hare drink tea with a sleeping Dormouse.
They say there is no room, but Alice sits down in a big chair.
The Hare offers her wine, but there is none, and they are rude to each other.
The Hatter says her hair is too long and asks a strange riddle.
Alice tries to guess the riddle, but they say that her words are wrong.
The Hatter looks at his watch and says that butter was bad for it.
Alice sees that the watch tells the date and not the time.
The Hatter says Alice does not know Time and cannot waste him.
Alice beats time in music, and the Hatter says Time hates that.
Time and the Hatter fought at the Queen's concert, so it is always six o'clock.
The Hatter says they move round the table, and the Hare asks for a story.
They wake the Dormouse, and it tells a story about three sisters in a well.
The sisters ate only treacle, so they were very ill.
The Dormouse says the sisters drew treacle from a treacle well.
The Hatter wants a clean cup, so they all move one chair.
Alice asks where they drew the treacle, and the answer is, “From the well.”
The sisters drew things that start with M, like mousetraps and the moon.
Alice is angry, and she walks away from the tea party.
She sees a door in a tree and goes through it.
She uses the key and a bit of mushroom, and she enters the garden.
In the garden, three men are painting white roses red.
They say they planted white roses by mistake, and the Queen is coming.
The Queen comes with soldiers, children and the Rabbit.
The Queen asks who Alice is, and Alice says her name politely.
The Queen is angry, but the King tells her that Alice is only a child.
The Queen orders the gardeners to lose their heads, but Alice hides them.
The Queen asks Alice if she can play croquet, and she says yes.
The Rabbit tells Alice that the Duchess is going to lose her head.
The Duchess hit the Queen, and Alice laughs out loud.
The Queen shouts, and everybody runs to their places for the game.
The croquet ground has ridges, and the balls are live hedgehogs.
Alice cannot hold her flamingo, and her hedgehog walks away.
Everyone plays at once, and the Queen shouts at them all the time.
Alice sees a grin in the air, and then the Cat's head appears.
Alice says the game is not fair, and the Cat asks about the Queen.
The King does not like the Cat, and he wants it taken away.
The Queen says to cut off the head, and the King goes for the executioner.
Alice looks for her hedgehog, but it is fighting, and her flamingo has gone.
A crowd gathers, and the King, the Queen and the executioner argue.
Alice says the Cat is the Duchess's, so the Queen sends for her.
The Duchess comes back, and she is now very friendly to Alice.
The Duchess says everything has a moral and leans her chin on Alice.
She says flamingos and mustard both bite, and she finds a moral.
The Duchess talks of morals, but the Queen comes and looks angry.
The Duchess runs away from the Queen, and the players go to prison.
The Queen asks about the Mock Turtle, and she leaves Alice with a Gryphon.
The Gryphon laughs, and then they find the Mock Turtle sobbing on a rock.
The Mock Turtle says that he was once a real Turtle, and then he cries.
The Mock Turtle says that he went to school in the sea.
His lessons are Reeling, Writhing and different kinds of Arithmetic.
Alice does not know the word, and the Mock Turtle names more lessons.
The Mock Turtle says that the lessons get shorter each day.
The Mock Turtle cries, and then he asks Alice about the Lobster Quadrille.
The Gryphon and the Mock Turtle jump about to show her the dance.
They dance around Alice, and the Mock Turtle sings a sad song.
Alice talks about the whiting, and the Gryphon explains about tails.
The Gryphon says that the whiting cleans boots and shoes under the sea.
The Mock Turtle says every fish needs a porpoise, and they want her story.
Alice tells her adventures, but the poem she says comes out wrong.
A cry says the trial is starting, so the Gryphon pulls Alice away.
Alice comes to a court, and the King and Queen sit on thrones.
The King is the judge, and twelve creatures are the jury.
Alice takes away the Lizard's pencil because it makes a bad noise.
The Rabbit reads out that the Knave of Hearts stole the Queen's tarts.
The first witness is the Hatter, and he has a teacup and some bread.
The Hatter says his hat is not his, and the King says it is stolen.
The Queen stares at him, and the Hatter shakes so much that he bites his cup.
The Hatter gives a confused answer about tea, and Alice starts to grow.
The Hatter runs out, and the Cook comes in with a box of pepper.
The Rabbit calls Alice, and she jumps up and upsets the jury-box.
Alice says sorry and puts the jurors back in their box.
The King wants all of them in place, so she turns the Lizard over.
The King asks what Alice knows, and she says that she knows nothing.
The Rabbit says the King means unimportant, and the King agrees.
The King reads a rule that says that nobody over a mile high may stay.
Alice says that the rule is new, and the King turns pale.
The Rabbit finds a paper, but the Knave says he did not write it.
The King says the paper proves it, but Alice says it proves nothing.
The Rabbit reads some verses, but Alice says they mean nothing.
The King finds a meaning in them and decides that the Knave cannot swim.
The King sees the tarts in the poem, and he thinks he has proof.
Alice says it is all nonsense, and the Queen shouts, but nobody moves.
Alice is her full size now, and she says they are only a pack of cards.
All the cards fly up and fall on Alice, and she screams.
Alice wakes on the river bank, with her head on her sister's lap.
Her sister wakes her, and Alice tells her about her strange dream.
Her sister kisses her and says that it is time to go to tea.
Alice runs home, thinking about the wonderful dream she has had.
Her sister sits on the bank and dreams about Wonderland.
She pictures Alice grown up, telling her stories to little children.
B1B2: Alice is sitting on the riverbank beside her sister, who is reading a book with no pictures and no conversations in it. Alice is very bored, and she wonders what use such a book can possibly be.
The day is so hot that Alice feels half asleep, and she cannot decide whether to make a daisy chain. Picking the flowers would mean getting up, and that seems like a lot of trouble.
Suddenly a White Rabbit with pink eyes runs close past her, muttering that he is going to be late. Alice does not think this is very strange, because she is almost dreaming anyway.
Then the Rabbit takes a watch out of his waistcoat pocket, looks at it and hurries on. Alice jumps up, because she has never before seen a rabbit with a waistcoat and a watch.

Full of curiosity, Alice runs across the field after him and sees him disappear into a large hole under the hedge. A moment later she is going in after him, and she never stops to think how she will get out again.

For a while the tunnel goes straight on, and then it suddenly dips down into what seems to be a very deep well. Either the well is very deep or Alice is falling very slowly, because she has plenty of time to look around.

The sides of the well are covered with cupboards and bookshelves, and she sees maps and pictures hanging on pegs. She takes a jar labelled orange marmalade from a shelf, but it is empty, so she puts it into a cupboard as she falls past.

After a fall like this, Alice thinks, she will not be afraid of tumbling down the stairs at home. She begins to talk about her cat Dinah, and she hopes someone will remember the saucer of milk at teatime.

Down, down, down she goes, getting sleepy and asking herself whether cats eat bats or bats eat cats. Then, all at once, she lands with a thump on a heap of sticks and dry leaves, and the fall is over.
Alice is not hurt at all, and she jumps to her feet and looks up, but it is dark overhead. In front of her is another long passage, and she sees the White Rabbit hurrying along it.

Alice runs after the Rabbit and hears him say that it is getting very late. When she turns the corner, he has completely disappeared, and she is standing in a long, low hall with lamps hanging from the roof.

There are doors all around the hall, but when Alice tries them, one after another, every single one is locked. She walks sadly down one side and up the other, wondering how she will ever get out again.

All at once she comes to a little three-legged table made of solid glass, and there is nothing on it except a tiny golden key. Alice thinks it must belong to one of the doors, but the locks are too big or the key is too small.
On her second trip round the hall, she finds a low curtain that she did not notice before. Behind it is a little door only fifteen inches high, and to her great delight the golden key fits the lock.

Alice opens the door and finds a small passage, not much bigger than a rat-hole. She kneels down and looks along it into the loveliest garden she has ever seen, with bright flower-beds and cool fountains.

She longs to leave the dark hall and wander among the flowers, but she cannot even get her head through the doorway. Poor Alice wishes she could shut up like a telescope, and she begins to think that few things are impossible.

There is no use waiting by the little door, so she goes back to the table, half hoping to find another key. Instead she finds a small bottle with a paper label round its neck, and the label says “Drink me” in large letters.

Alice is a careful girl, so she checks that the bottle is not marked poison before she drinks anything. It is safe, and the taste is a mixture of cherry tart, custard, pineapple, roast turkey and hot buttered toast.

Alice feels as if she is closing up like a telescope, and she is right, because she is now ten inches tall. She is glad, but she waits a moment in case she shrinks away completely, like a candle going out.

Alice reaches the door and finds that she has forgotten the key, which is now far too high on the glass table. She sits down and cries, but then she sees a small glass box with a cake marked “Eat me” in currants.
The cake tastes sweet, and Alice eats it all, and then she begins to grow taller and taller. She is so surprised that she forgets how to speak properly and cries out, “Curiouser and curiouser!”

Her feet are so far away that she can hardly see them, and she says goodbye to them in a sad voice. She wonders who will put on her shoes and stockings now, because she certainly cannot do it herself.
Alice decides she must be kind to her feet and send them a new pair of boots every Christmas. Then she laughs, because it would be so strange to send a parcel to her own right foot.
Just then her head hits the roof of the hall, and she finds that she is more than nine feet tall. She quickly picks up the little golden key and hurries to the garden door.
It is a poor result, because she can only lie on one side and look at the garden with one eye. Getting through the door is more hopeless than ever, so she sits down and begins to cry.

Alice tells herself that a big girl like her should be ashamed to cry like this, but she goes on crying anyway. Her tears run across the floor until there is a pool four inches deep around her, reaching halfway down the hall.
After a while she hears a pattering of feet in the distance and quickly dries her eyes. It is the White Rabbit, splendidly dressed and carrying white gloves in one hand and a large fan in the other.

He is muttering that the Duchess will be furious if he keeps her waiting. When Alice says timidly, “If you please, sir,” the Rabbit jumps with fright, drops the gloves and the fan and runs into the darkness.

Alice picks up the fan and the gloves, and because the hall is very hot, she begins to fan herself while she talks. Then she notices that she has put on one of the Rabbit's little gloves, and she must be shrinking again.
She works out that the fan is the cause, so she drops it just in time to avoid shrinking to nothing. She runs to the little door, but it is shut again, and then she slips and falls into salt water.

Alice thinks she has fallen into the sea, and she remembers that you can always go home by train from the seaside. Then she sees that she is in the pool of her own tears, and she wishes she had not cried so much.

Something is splashing about in the pool, and at first she thinks it is a walrus, but it is only a Mouse. Alice decides that the Mouse might be able to talk, so she says, “O Mouse, do you know the way out of this pool?”

The Mouse only stares at her, so Alice tries French, which is the first sentence in her lesson book, and asks where her cat is. The Mouse leaps out of the water and shivers with fright, and Alice quickly says she forgot that mice do not like cats.
The Mouse cries out in a shrill voice that nobody could like cats if they were in his place. Alice praises Dinah, who is so quiet and so good at catching mice, and the Mouse's fur stands on end.

Alice makes things worse by speaking of a terrier that kills rats, and the Mouse swims away in a rage. She promises not to mention cats or dogs again, so he comes back and agrees to tell his story on the shore.
It is time to leave, because the pool is crowded with birds and animals that have fallen in. Alice leads the way to the shore, followed by a Duck, a Dodo, a Lory, an Eaglet and many others.

On the bank the creatures look wet and cross, and their first question is how to get dry. Soon Alice is chatting like an old friend, and she argues with the Lory, who says he is older and knows better.

The Mouse seems to be an important person among them, so when he calls for silence, they all sit down in a ring. He says that he will soon make them dry, and he begins the driest piece of history he knows, about William the Conqueror.
The Mouse's story does not help, and the creatures stay as wet as ever. At last the Dodo stands and uses very long words to suggest stronger remedies, and the Eaglet hides a smile.

The Eaglet tells the Dodo to speak English, because he does not know half those long words, and some birds laugh. The Dodo, offended, says that the best way to get dry is a Caucus-race, and Alice asks what that is.
The Dodo marks out a course in the shape of a circle, saying that the exact shape does not matter. Then all the creatures are placed along the track, here and there, with no particular order.
Nobody says “One, two, three, go,” so they all start running whenever they like and stop whenever they like. It is hard to know when the race is over, but after about half an hour they are quite dry.

The Dodo suddenly shouts that the race is over, and they all crowd round him, panting and asking who has won. He thinks for a long time with one finger on his forehead, and then he says that everybody has won and all must have prizes.

Everyone asks who will give the prizes, and the Dodo points at Alice, so the whole crowd gathers round her. In despair she pulls a box of sweets from her pocket, and she hands them round, one for each.

The animals say that Alice must have a prize too, and the Dodo asks what else she has in her pocket. She has only a thimble, so she gives it to him, and he presents it back to her very solemnly while everyone cheers.

Alice thinks it is all very silly, but they look so serious that she does not dare to laugh. The sweets cause confusion, because the big birds cannot taste theirs and the small birds choke and need patting on the back.
When it is over, they sit in a ring and ask the Mouse to tell them more. Alice reminds him why he hates cats and dogs, and the Mouse sighs and says that his tale is long and sad.

Alice looks at the Mouse's long tail and wonders why he calls his tale sad, so she puzzles over it instead of listening. The Mouse angrily asks what she is thinking about, and when she mentions the fifth bend, he storms off.

Alice calls after the Mouse to come back, but he only shakes his head and walks on. Then she says aloud that she wishes Dinah were here, and when she explains that Dinah catches birds, they all hurry away.

Alone, Alice sits down sadly and cries, because nobody in this place seems to like her cat. After a while she hears pattering footsteps and looks up, and the White Rabbit is trotting back, searching anxiously for something.

The Rabbit trots slowly back, looking worried and muttering that the Duchess will have him executed if he cannot find his gloves and fan. Alice starts to look for them too, but everything has changed since her swim, and the great hall and the glass table have gone.

Soon the Rabbit sees her searching and calls out angrily, “Why, Mary Ann, what are you doing out here?” He orders her to fetch gloves and a fan, and Alice is so frightened that she runs off without explaining.

She runs on, thinking that he took her for his housemaid and will be surprised to learn who she is. Soon she finds a neat little house with the Rabbit's name on a brass plate, and she goes in and hurries upstairs.
She thinks it is very odd to be running errands for a rabbit, and she imagines Dinah giving her orders next. On a table by the window she finds a fan and several pairs of tiny white gloves.

As she picks up the fan and gloves, she sees a little bottle by the looking-glass, and this time it has no label. She drinks it anyway, because something interesting always happens when she eats or drinks anything.

She hopes it will make her larger, because she is tired of being such a tiny thing, and it does, much sooner than she expects. Before she has drunk half of it, her head presses against the ceiling, and she wishes she had stopped.
It is too late, because she keeps on growing, and soon she has to kneel, and then she has to lie down on the floor. Still she grows, so she puts one arm out of the window and one foot up the chimney.

Luckily the magic bottle has done its work, and Alice grows no larger, but she is very uncomfortable and sees no way out. She wonders whether she will ever grow older than she is now, and she decides that having lessons all her life would be dreadful.

The Rabbit shouts outside for his gloves, and Alice trembles so much that she shakes the whole house. He cannot open the door because her elbow is pressed against it, so he goes to the window, and she snatches at him.

Alice hears a shriek, a fall and a crash of breaking glass, and she guesses that the Rabbit has landed in a cucumber frame. Then he angrily calls his gardener Pat, who says he is digging for apples and that there is an arm in the window.

Alice waits for a while and then spreads out her hand and snatches at the air again. This time there are two little shrieks and more breaking glass, and she wonders how many cucumber frames there can possibly be.
After a long wait, she hears the rumbling of little cartwheels and a crowd of voices all talking at once. They argue about ladders, ropes and a loose slate, until something falls with a loud crash.

Then she hears the voices say that Bill must go down the chimney, and she tells herself that she would not like to be Bill. The fireplace is narrow, but she thinks she can still kick a little, so she draws her foot down the chimney and waits.

Presently she hears a small animal scrambling in the chimney just above her, and she gives it one sharp kick. The crowd outside shouts that there goes Bill, and he shoots up into the sky like a rocket.

The Rabbit orders them to catch Bill, and a weak, squeaking voice says that something hit it like a jack-in-the-box. When the Rabbit says they must burn the house down, Alice shouts that she will set Dinah on them.
A shower of little pebbles rattles in through the window, and some of them hit Alice in the face. She shouts at them to stop, and then she sees that the pebbles are turning into little cakes.

If she eats one of the cakes, she thinks, it must change her size, and it can only make her smaller. She swallows one and shrinks at once, and then she runs out to a crowd of little animals and poor Bill.

They all rush at Alice when she appears, but she runs as hard as she can and soon finds herself in a thick wood. She tells herself that she must grow to her proper size and then find the way into the lovely garden.

It is a good plan, but she has no idea how to begin, and then a sharp little bark makes her look up. An enormous puppy is looking down at her with huge round eyes, trying feebly to touch her with one paw.
Alice holds out a little stick, and the puppy leaps for it while she dodges behind a thistle. When the puppy sits down far away, she runs until the barking is faint and rests against a buttercup.
Alice sits by the buttercup and wonders how she can grow to her proper size again. She looks for something to eat or drink, and then she sees a large mushroom as tall as she is.

She looks under it, behind it and on both sides, and then she thinks that she had better look on top. She stands on tiptoe and peeps over the edge, and her eyes meet those of a large blue Caterpillar.
The Caterpillar is sitting with its arms folded, smoking a long pipe and taking no notice of her. At last it takes the pipe out of its mouth and asks in a sleepy voice, “Who are you?”

Alice answers shyly that she hardly knows, because she was one person this morning and has been changed several times since. The Caterpillar tells her to explain herself, but she says she cannot, because she is not herself.

Alice says that changing size so often is confusing, and that the Caterpillar will find it strange when it becomes a butterfly. The Caterpillar says it will not, and then it asks again who she is, so she turns away angrily.

The Caterpillar calls her back, telling her that it has something important to say, and it tells her to keep her temper. Then, after puffing smoke for some minutes, it asks whether she thinks she is changed, and tells her to recite a poem.

Alice folds her hands and begins to recite “You are old, Father William”, but all the words come out wrong. She talks about an old man who stands on his head, and she gets the rest of the poem very mixed up.

The Caterpillar says that she has said it all wrong from beginning to end, and then it asks what size she wants to be. Alice says that she only wants to be a little larger, because three inches is such a wretched height, and the Caterpillar rears up angrily.

“You will get used to it in time,” says the Caterpillar, and it puts the pipe back in its mouth and smokes in silence. After a minute it yawns, crawls down from the mushroom and says that one side will make her taller and the other shorter.

Alice asks which side of what, and the Caterpillar answers that it means the mushroom, and then it disappears. The mushroom is perfectly round, so she stretches her arms around it and breaks off a piece with each hand.

Alice nibbles a little of the right-hand piece, and a moment later she feels a blow under her chin, because it has hit her foot. She is shrinking fast, so she quickly eats some of the other piece, though her chin is squeezed against her foot.

Alice is glad that her head is free at last, but she is alarmed to find that her shoulders have disappeared. When she looks down, she sees a very long neck rising like a stalk out of a sea of green leaves.

She cannot see her hands, so she bends her neck down like a snake and finds that the leaves are tree tops. Just as she dives in, a sharp hiss makes her draw back, because a pigeon flies into her face.

The Pigeon screams that Alice is a serpent and beats her with its wings, but she says she is nothing of the kind. The Pigeon sobs that it has tried tree roots, banks and hedges, but nothing ever suits those serpents.

The Pigeon says that hatching eggs is enough trouble without watching for serpents day and night, and it has not slept for three weeks. It chose the highest tree in the wood, and it thought it was safe, but now serpents come wriggling down from the sky.

Alice says that she is only a little girl, but the Pigeon replies that no little girl has a neck like hers. Alice admits that she has tasted eggs, so the Pigeon says that she must be a kind of serpent.

The Pigeon settles down on its nest in a bad mood, and Alice crouches among the trees, untwisting her neck from the branches. Then she remembers the mushroom in her hands and nibbles at both pieces until she is her usual height again.

She feels very strange at first because she has not been the right size for so long, but she soon gets used to it. Then she comes upon a little house about four feet high, so she nibbles the right-hand piece again until she is nine inches tall.

While she wonders what to do, a footman in uniform runs out of the wood and knocks loudly on the door. He has the face of a fish, and the door is opened by another footman with a round face and big eyes like a frog.

The Fish-Footman hands over a great letter, announcing an invitation from the Queen for the Duchess to play croquet. The Frog-Footman repeats it, and they bow so low that their curls tangle, so Alice runs off to laugh.
Alice walks up to the house and knocks, but the Footman says there is no use in knocking. He is on the same side of the door as she is, and there is so much noise inside that nobody could hear.
There is a howling and a sneezing inside, and now and then a crash, as if a dish has broken. Alice asks how to get in, but the Footman stares at the sky, until a plate flies out and breaks on a tree.

The Footman goes on as if nothing has happened, and he says that he will sit there for days and days. When Alice asks what she should do, he says, “Anything you like,” and starts to whistle, so she opens the door and goes in.

The door leads into a smoky kitchen, where the Duchess sits nursing a baby and the cook stirs a cauldron. There is too much pepper in the air, and Alice and the Duchess sneeze and the baby sneezes and howls.

Only the cook and a large cat on the hearth do not sneeze, and the cat grins from ear to ear. Alice asks why the cat grins, and the Duchess answers that it is a Cheshire cat and tells her that she does not know much.
Alice does not like the Duchess's tone, so she tries to change the subject. Then the Cook throws everything at the Duchess and the baby, and Alice cries out to mind the baby's nose.

The Duchess growls that the world would go round faster if everyone minded their own business. Alice begins to explain about day and night, but the Duchess says to chop off her head and sings a lullaby.

While she sings a second verse, the Duchess tosses the baby up and down, and the poor thing howls. Then she flings it to Alice and hurries out to play croquet, and the Cook throws a frying-pan after her.

The baby is shaped like a starfish, but Alice learns how to hold it and carries it out into the open air. She thinks they will kill it if she leaves it behind, and when she says so aloud, the baby grunts.

The baby has a turned-up nose and very small eyes, and Alice warns it not to turn into a pig. When it grunts again, there can be no mistake, so she sets it down and watches it trot away into the wood.

Alice thinks that some children she knows would make good pigs, and then she sees the Cheshire Cat on a branch. It grins at her, and although it looks kind, it has long claws and many teeth, so she is respectful.
“Cheshire Puss,” she begins timidly, because she does not know if the Cat will like the name, but it only grins a little wider. She asks whether it can tell her which way she ought to go from here.
The Cat says that it depends on where she wants to get to, and Alice says she does not much care. Then it does not matter, says the Cat, because she will get somewhere if she walks long enough.

Alice asks what sort of people live around here, and the Cat waves its right paw and says that a Hatter lives in that direction. Then it waves its left paw and says that a March Hare lives that way, and it adds that they are both mad.

Alice says she does not want to go among mad people, but the Cat says that she cannot help it, because everyone is mad here. When she asks how it knows that she is mad, it says that she must be, or she would not have come.
The Cat says a dog is not mad, because a dog growls when angry and wags its tail when pleased. The Cat does the opposite, so it must be mad, but Alice says that is purring.

The Cat asks whether Alice will play croquet with the Queen, and she says she has not been invited. The Cat says that she will see it there and vanishes, and it soon returns to ask what happened to the baby.
After a moment the Cat appears once more and asks whether she said pig or fig. This time it vanishes slowly, beginning with its tail and ending with its grin, which stays in the air for a while.

Alice walks on, thinking that she has often seen a cat without a grin but never a grin without a cat. Soon she sees the March Hare's house, because the chimneys are shaped like ears and the roof is covered with fur.

The house is so large that Alice nibbles more mushroom first and grows to about two feet high. Even so, she walks up timidly, wondering whether the March Hare is raving mad and wishing she had visited the Hatter instead.

A table is set under a tree in front of the house, and the March Hare and the Hatter are having tea. A Dormouse sits fast asleep between them, and they rest their elbows on it as if it were a cushion.
The table is large, but the three of them crowd into one corner and say that there is no room. Alice says there is plenty of room and sits down in a big armchair at the end.
The March Hare invites her to have some wine, but there is only tea on the table. Alice calls it rude to offer wine that is not there, and the Hare calls it rude to sit down uninvited.

The Hatter has been looking at Alice with great curiosity, and he says that her hair wants cutting. Alice replies that it is rude to make personal remarks, and the Hatter asks why a raven is like a writing-desk.

Alice says she thinks that she can guess the answer, and the Hare says that she should say what she means. She says that she means what she says, but the Hatter says that it is not the same thing at all.
The Hatter takes out his watch, looks at it in a worried way and asks what day of the month it is. Alice says it is the fourth, and he sighs that it is two days wrong and blames the butter.
Alice thinks it is a funny watch, because it tells the day of the month but not the time. The Hatter asks if her watch tells the year, and she says no, because the year stays the same for so long.
Nobody knows the answer, so Alice gives up and says that they waste time on riddles without answers. The Hatter says that Time is a person, and she would not waste him if she knew him.
Alice says that she has never spoken to Time, but she beats time in her music lessons. The Hatter says that Time will not stand beating, but a friend of Time's can make the clock go as she likes.
The Hatter tells how he and Time quarrelled last March, when he sang at a concert given by the Queen. The Queen shouted that he was murdering the time, and since then it has always been six o'clock.

The Hatter says that they keep moving round the table when the cups are used, so they can have clean ones. Alice asks what happens when they come back to the beginning, but the Hare yawns and says he is tired and would like a story.

Alice does not know any stories, so they pinch the Dormouse awake on both sides and ask it to tell one. The Dormouse says it was not asleep and begins a story about Elsie, Lacie and Tillie, three sisters who lived in a well.

Alice asks what the sisters ate, and the Dormouse says they lived on treacle, so Alice says that they must have been ill. The Dormouse agrees, but when Alice asks why they lived in a well, the Hare tells her to take more tea.

Alice says that she has had nothing yet, so she cannot take more, and the Hatter says she means she cannot take less. The Dormouse says that it was a treacle well, and it sulks when Alice says there is no such thing.

Alice apologises humbly, and the Dormouse agrees to go on, saying that the sisters were learning to draw, and that they drew treacle. Then the Hatter wants a clean cup, so they all move one place, and Alice gets the Hare's seat and his spilled milk.

Alice asks where the sisters drew the treacle from, and the Hatter says that it came from a treacle well, of course. Alice says that they were in the well, and the Dormouse says that of course they were, well in.

The Dormouse yawns and says that the sisters drew all manner of things that begin with M, such as mousetraps, the moon, memory and muchness. Alice asks if anyone has seen a drawing of a muchness, but the Hatter says that then she should not talk.

Alice cannot bear this rudeness and gets up and walks off, and the Dormouse falls asleep at once. She looks back and sees them putting the Dormouse in the teapot, and she calls it the stupidest tea-party ever.
As she walks through the wood, she sees a door in one of the trees. She says everything is curious today, so she goes in and finds herself in the long hall again.

This time she is wiser, and she takes the golden key and unlocks the little door. She nibbles the mushroom until she is a foot high, and at last she walks into the garden, among the flowers and fountains.
