Near the entrance to the garden is a large rose tree with white roses on it, and three gardeners are busily painting them red. Alice goes closer and hears them quarrelling about who splashed paint on whom.

The gardeners explain that they planted a white rose tree by mistake, and they have to make it red before the Queen sees it. Then one of them shouts that the Queen is coming, and they all throw themselves flat on their faces.

First come ten soldiers with clubs, then ten courtiers covered with diamonds, and then ten royal children covered with hearts. After them come the guests, including the White Rabbit, and last of all come the King and Queen of Hearts.

Alice wonders whether she should lie down like the gardeners, but she has never heard of such a rule, so she stands still. The Queen asks who she is, and Alice answers politely, but she tells herself that they are only a pack of cards.

The Queen points at the gardeners lying on their faces and asks who they are, but she cannot tell them apart from her own soldiers. Alice says it is no business of hers, and the King begs the angry Queen to remember that she is only a child.

The Queen looks at the painted roses, orders the gardeners to lose their heads and walks on, leaving three soldiers to carry out the sentence. Alice puts the gardeners into a large flower-pot, so the soldiers search for a while and then march off.

The Queen shouts to the soldiers to ask whether the heads are off, and they shout back that the heads are gone. Then she asks Alice if she can play croquet, and Alice shouts yes, and she joins the procession, wondering what will happen next.

A timid voice at her side says that it is a very fine day, and Alice sees the White Rabbit peeping anxiously at her. He looks over his shoulder, stands on tiptoe and whispers in her ear that the Duchess is under sentence of execution.

Alice asks what the Duchess did, and the Rabbit tells her that she boxed the Queen's ears. Alice gives a little scream of laughter, and the Rabbit begs her to be quiet, because the Queen will hear and the Duchess came late.
The Queen shouts at everyone to get to their places, and people run about in all directions, tumbling over each other. After a minute or two they settle down, and the game begins.
Alice has never seen such a curious croquet-ground, because it is all ridges and furrows. The balls are live hedgehogs, the mallets are live flamingos, and the soldiers bend over to make the arches.

Alice cannot manage her flamingo, because it twists its neck round and looks up at her with a puzzled face. When she gets its head down again, she finds that the hedgehog has unrolled itself and is crawling away.

The players all play at once, quarrelling and fighting for the hedgehogs, and the Queen is soon in a furious passion. She stamps about and orders someone's head off about once a minute, and Alice begins to feel uneasy.
Alice looks for a way to escape, but then she sees a strange shape in the air. After watching for a minute, she sees that it is a grin, and then the whole head of the Cheshire Cat appears.
Alice puts down her flamingo and tells the Cat that nobody plays fairly, and that everything in the game is alive. Then the Cat asks in a low voice how she likes the Queen.
Alice says that she does not like her, but she sees the Queen listening and quickly changes her words. The Queen smiles and passes on, and the King stares at the Cat's head and says he dislikes it.

The Cat will not kiss the King's hand, so the King says that it must be removed and calls to the Queen. The Queen orders its head off, as she does with every difficulty, and the King hurries to fetch the executioner.
Alice decides to go back to the game and looks for her hedgehog, but it is fighting with another one. Her flamingo has gone to the other side of the garden, where it is trying to fly into a tree.
By the time Alice has caught the flamingo, the fight is over, and she goes back to the Cat. A large crowd has gathered around it, and the executioner, the King and the Queen are all arguing at once.

The executioner says you cannot cut off a head without a body, and the King says that you can. Alice says that the Cat belongs to the Duchess, so the Queen sends for her, and the Cat's head fades away.

The Duchess takes Alice's arm affectionately and says she is glad to see her again. Alice is happy to find her in a good mood, and she decides that it was probably only the pepper that made her so fierce.

Alice thinks that pepper makes people hot-tempered, and she says she will never have it in her kitchen. The Duchess says that everything has a moral, if only you can find it, and she rests her sharp chin on Alice's shoulder.

The Duchess says that flamingos and mustard both bite, and the moral is that birds of a feather flock together. Alice says that mustard is not a bird, and the Duchess agrees that it is a mineral, and so she finds a new moral.

The Duchess goes on finding morals, and she is pleased with everything Alice says, until she begins to say her favourite word. Suddenly her voice dies away and her arm trembles, because the Queen is standing in front of them, frowning like a thunderstorm.

The Queen warns the Duchess that either she or her head must go, and the Duchess chooses and is gone in a moment. Then the Queen orders Alice back to the game, and soon she has sentenced every player to execution, apart from the King and Alice.

The Queen asks whether Alice has seen the Mock Turtle, and Alice says that she does not even know what one is. The Queen says that Mock Turtle soup is made from it, leaves Alice with a sleeping Gryphon, and goes to see to her executions.
The Gryphon wakes up and laughs when the Queen has gone, because nobody is ever really executed. Soon they see the Mock Turtle sitting on a ledge of rock, sighing as if his heart would break.
The Gryphon says that Alice wants to hear his history, and the Mock Turtle tells her to sit and not speak. After some silence he says that he was once a real Turtle, and then he sobs for a long time.

The Mock Turtle says that he went to school in the sea, and the master was an old Turtle called Tortoise. Alice asks why he was called Tortoise, and the Mock Turtle says that it was because he taught us.

The Mock Turtle says that they had the best education, and he asks whether Alice had extras at her school, like French and washing. He says that his own course was the regular one, which began with Reeling and Writhing, followed by Ambition, Distraction, Uglification and Derision.

Alice says that she has never heard of uglifying, and the Gryphon is amazed, because she must know what to beautify means. The Mock Turtle goes on with Mystery, Seaography, and Drawling, Stretching and Fainting in Coils, which was taught by an old conger-eel.

Alice asks how many hours a day they did lessons, and the Mock Turtle says ten the first day, nine the next, and so on. The Gryphon says that is why they are called lessons, because they lessen from day to day, and the eleventh day is a holiday.

The Mock Turtle tries to speak, but sobs choke his voice, and the Gryphon shakes him and thumps his back. At last he says that she may not have seen a lobster, so she cannot know how delightful a Lobster Quadrille is.

The Gryphon says that you form a line along the sea-shore and advance twice, each with a lobster as partner. Then you change lobsters, throw them out to sea, swim after them and turn a somersault, and that is the first figure.

Alice says it must be a pretty dance, so the Mock Turtle says that they can try the first figure without any lobsters. They dance solemnly around her, sometimes treading on her toes, while the Mock Turtle sings very slowly and sadly about a whiting and a snail.

When the dance is over, Alice says that she likes the song about the whiting, and the Mock Turtle asks whether she has seen them. She says that they have their tails in their mouths, and the Gryphon says that they were thrown out to sea.

The Gryphon asks whether Alice knows why it is called a whiting, and when she does not, he says that it cleans boots and shoes. Alice says that her shoes are done with blacking, but under the sea, he says, they are done with a whiting.

Alice says that she would have told the porpoise to keep back, but no wise fish goes anywhere without one. Alice says he must mean purpose, but he says he means what he says, and the Gryphon asks to hear her adventures.

Alice tells her adventures, beginning with the White Rabbit, and she feels nervous at first, but she gains courage as the creatures listen. When she says that her poem came out all different, the Gryphon tells her to recite one now, and the words come out very queer.

The Mock Turtle says that what Alice recited sounds like nonsense, and Alice sits down with her face in her hands. He starts to sing about soup, but a cry says that the trial is beginning, and the Gryphon hurries Alice away.

Alice arrives with the Gryphon at a court where the King and Queen of Hearts are sitting on thrones, with a great crowd around them. The Knave of Hearts stands in chains with a soldier on each side, and the White Rabbit holds a trumpet and a scroll.

The King is wearing his crown over a wig, and he is the judge, which does not look comfortable. The jurors are twelve creatures of all kinds, and they write busily on slates, though nothing has happened yet.

One of the jurors is Bill the Lizard, whose pencil squeaks so much that Alice cannot bear it. Alice sneaks behind him and snatches it away, and the poor Lizard writes with his finger for the rest of the day.

The King tells the Rabbit to read the accusation, and the Rabbit blows three blasts on the trumpet and unrolls the scroll. He reads that the Queen of Hearts made some tarts, and that the Knave of Hearts stole them and took them away.

The King tells the jury to consider their verdict, but the Rabbit says that there is a great deal more to come before that. The first witness is the Hatter, who comes in with a teacup in one hand and a piece of bread and butter in the other.

The Hatter says that he is sorry to bring these in, but he had not finished his tea when he was sent for. The King tells him to take off his hat, but the Hatter says it is not his, so the King says it is stolen.

The Hatter explains that he keeps hats to sell and has none of his own, because he is a hatter. The Queen puts on her spectacles and stares, and he trembles so much that he bites his teacup instead of his bread.

The King tells the Hatter to give his evidence or be executed, and the Hatter says he is a poor man. He says that the twinkling of the tea began it all, and the King is baffled, while Alice begins to grow.

The Dormouse, who is sitting beside Alice, complains that she is squeezing it, and she says that she cannot help growing. The Hatter is told that he may go, and he runs out so fast that he leaves his shoes behind.

The Cook comes in with a pepper-box and says that tarts are made of pepper, but a sleepy voice says treacle. In the confusion the Rabbit calls Alice as the next witness, and she jumps up and upsets the jury-box.

Alice cries that she is very sorry and hurries to pick up the jurors, who have tumbled all over the floor. She puts them back as fast as she can, because she fears that they will die like a goldfish she once upset.

The King says solemnly that the trial cannot go on until every juror is in his place, and he looks hard at Alice. She sees that she has put the Lizard in head first, so she gently turns him the right way up.
When the jurors have recovered, the King asks Alice what she knows about the matter. She says nothing, and the King asks whether she knows nothing whatever, and she says nothing whatever.

The King says that is very important, but the White Rabbit says politely that he means unimportant, and he makes faces at him. The King mutters important, unimportant, important to himself, as if he is trying to find out which word sounds best.

The King calls for silence and reads out Rule Forty-two, which says that anyone more than a mile high must leave the court. Everybody looks at Alice, and she says that she is not a mile high, but the Queen says that she is nearly two miles.

Alice says that she will not go, and that the rule is not a regular one, because the King has just invented it. The King says it is the oldest rule in the book, so Alice says it must be Rule One, and he turns pale.

The King tells the jury to consider their verdict, but the White Rabbit jumps up and says that a paper has just been found. It looks like a letter from the prisoner, but nobody signed it, and the Knave says that he did not write it.

The King says that if the Knave did not sign it, it only makes things worse, because he must have meant some mischief. The Queen cries that this proves his guilt, but Alice says that it proves nothing, because nobody even knows what the verses are about.
The King tells the Rabbit to read the verses, and he says to begin at the beginning and stop at the end. The verses are a muddle of he and she and I and they, and Alice says that they mean nothing.

The King says that no meaning saves a world of trouble, but he seems to see some meaning in the verses after all. He asks the Knave if he can swim, and the Knave sadly asks if he looks like it, being made of cardboard.

The King, delighted, says that the verses mention the tarts, and that this is the best evidence yet. The Queen says furiously that the jury must not decide yet, because the sentence must come first and the verdict afterwards.

Alice says that this is stuff and nonsense, and that it is ridiculous to have the sentence first. The Queen turns purple and orders her head off, but nobody moves, because they are only a pack of cards.
Alice has grown to her full size by now, and she is not at all afraid of the angry Queen. She tells the court that nobody cares for them, because they are nothing but a pack of cards.
At this the whole pack rises up into the air and comes flying down upon her. Alice gives a little scream, half of fright and half of anger, and she tries to beat them off.
Suddenly Alice finds herself lying on the riverbank with her head on her sister's lap. Her sister is gently brushing away some dead leaves that have fluttered down on her face.
Her sister says that it is time to wake up, because Alice has had a long sleep. Alice says that she has had a curious dream, and she tells her sister all her strange adventures.
When she has finished, her sister kisses her and says that it was certainly a curious dream. She tells Alice to run in and have her tea, because it is getting late.

Her chin was pressed so tightly against her foot that she could scarcely open her mouth, but at last she managed to swallow a morsel of the left-hand bit.

Alice remarked with delight that her head was free at last, but her joy changed to alarm a moment later when she found that her shoulders were nowhere to be seen. All she could see, when she looked down, was an immense length of neck, which seemed to rise like a stalk out of a sea of green foliage lying far below her. She wondered what all that greenery could be, and where her poor hands had gone, and why she could no longer glimpse them.

There was no chance of getting her hands up to her head, so she tried to get her head down to them, and she was delighted to find that her neck would bend about like a serpent. She had just succeeded in curving it into a graceful zigzag and was about to dive among the leaves, which proved to be the tops of the trees under which she had wandered. At that moment a sharp hiss made her draw back in a hurry, for a large pigeon had flown into her face and was beating her violently with its wings.

The Pigeon screamed that she was a serpent, and Alice indignantly answered that she was nothing of the kind and begged to be let alone. The Pigeon repeated the word in a more subdued tone, and added with a kind of sob that it had tried every way and nothing seemed to suit them. It had tried the roots of trees and it had tried banks and hedges, it said, but those serpents were never to be pleased.

Alice grew more and more puzzled, but she thought there was no use in saying anything until the Pigeon had finished. As if it were not enough trouble hatching eggs, the Pigeon complained, it had to be on the lookout for serpents night and day, and it had not had a wink of sleep these three weeks. It had taken the highest tree in the wood, and it had hoped to be free of them at last, but they must needs come wriggling down from the sky.

“I am not a serpent, I tell you,” said Alice, “I am only a little girl.” “A likely story indeed,” said the Pigeon with deep contempt, for it had seen many little girls in its time but never one with a neck like that. When Alice admitted, being a truthful child, that she had tasted eggs, the Pigeon argued that little girls who ate them were a kind of serpent, and Alice was silent, for the idea was new to her.

The Pigeon told her sulkily to be off and settled down into its nest again. Alice crouched among the trees as well as she could, for her neck kept getting tangled in the branches, and every now and then she had to stop and untwist it. After a while she remembered the pieces of mushroom still in her hands and nibbled first at one and then at the other, until she had brought herself down to her usual height.

It was so long since she had been anywhere near her right size that it felt quite strange at first, but she got used to it in a few minutes and began talking to herself as usual. She remarked that half her plan was done now and that the next thing was to get into that beautiful garden, though she could not think how. Just then she came upon an open place with a little house about four feet high, and she nibbled the mushroom until she was nine inches tall, so as not to frighten whoever lived there.

For a minute or two she stood looking at the house and wondering what to do next, when suddenly a footman in livery came running out of the wood. She took him for a footman only because of his livery, for judging by his face alone she would have called him a fish. He rapped loudly at the door with his knuckles, and it was opened by another footman in livery, who had a round face, large eyes like a frog, and powdered hair that curled all over his head.

She felt very curious to know what was going on, so she crept a little way out of the wood to listen, and she saw the Fish-Footman produce from under his arm a great letter nearly as large as himself. In a solemn tone he announced that it was an invitation from the Queen for the Duchess to play croquet, and the Frog-Footman repeated the message with the words slightly changed. Then they both bowed so low that their curls got entangled, and Alice laughed so much that she had to run back into the wood for fear of being heard.

Alice walked up to the house and knocked timidly, but the Footman informed her that there was no use in knocking, for two reasons. First, he was on the same side of the door as she was, and second, they were making such a noise inside that no one could possibly hear her. A constant howling and sneezing came from within, and every now and then a great crash, as if a dish or a kettle had been broken to pieces.

Alice asked, a little desperately, how she was to get in at all, but the Footman went on without attending to her. He remarked that there might be some sense in her knocking if they had the door between them, and all the time he looked up into the sky, which Alice thought decidedly uncivil. Just then the door of the house opened, and a large plate skimmed out, straight at his head, grazing his nose and breaking to pieces against a tree behind him.

The Footman announced that he would sit there for days and days, and when Alice asked what she was to do, he told her to do anything she liked and began to whistle. Alice decided desperately that there was no use talking to him, for he was perfectly idiotic. And with that she opened the door and went in, ready for whatever she might find inside.

The door led straight into a large kitchen, which was full of smoke from one end to the other. The Duchess was sitting on a three-legged stool in the middle, nursing a baby, and the cook was leaning over the fire, stirring a great cauldron of soup. There was certainly too much pepper in the air, and Alice sneezed so much that she could hardly speak, while even the Duchess sneezed from time to time, and the baby sneezed and howled without a moment's pause.

The only creatures in the kitchen that did not sneeze were the cook and a large cat, which sat on the hearth and grinned from ear to ear. Alice asked rather timidly why the cat grinned like that, and the Duchess answered that it was a Cheshire cat, and that was why. The Duchess then shouted a word at the baby with such sudden violence that Alice jumped, and when Alice said politely that she had not known cats could grin, the Duchess retorted that they all could and most did.

Alice did not at all like the tone of this remark and thought it would be as well to introduce some other subject of conversation. But before she could fix upon one, the cook took the cauldron off the fire and began throwing everything within reach at the Duchess and the baby, first the fire-irons, then a shower of saucepans, plates and dishes. The Duchess took no notice, even when she was hit, and Alice jumped up and down in an agony of terror, begging them to mind what they were doing, as a saucepan flew within an inch of the baby's nose.

“If everybody minded their own business,” said the Duchess in a hoarse growl, “the world would go round a deal faster than it does.” Alice, glad of a chance to show off her knowledge, began to explain about the earth and day and night, but the Duchess cut her short by saying that someone should chop off her head. She then began to nurse the baby again, singing a sort of lullaby and giving it a violent shake at the end of every line.

While she sang the second verse, she kept tossing the baby violently up and down, and the poor little thing howled so loud that Alice could hardly hear the words. “Here, you may nurse it a bit, if you like,” said the Duchess, flinging the baby at her, “I must go and get ready to play croquet with the Queen.” She hurried out of the room, and the cook threw a frying-pan after her, which just missed her.

Alice caught the baby with some difficulty, as it was a queer-shaped little creature that held out its arms and legs in all directions, just like a starfish, and it snorted like a steam engine. As soon as she had discovered the proper way of nursing it, which was to twist it into a sort of knot and hold tight to its right ear and left foot, she carried it out into the open air. She felt sure they would kill it in a day or two if she left it behind, and when she said so aloud, the little thing grunted in reply.

The baby grunted again, and Alice looked anxiously into its face and saw that it had a very turned-up nose, much more like a snout than a real nose. She told it that if it was going to turn into a pig, she would have nothing more to do with it, but it grunted again so violently that there could be no mistake. So she set the little creature down and felt quite relieved to see it trot away quietly into the wood, and she thought it would have made a dreadfully ugly child but rather a handsome pig.

Alice was still thinking how well some of the children she knew would make pigs when she was a little startled to see the Cheshire Cat sitting on a bough of a tree nearby. The Cat grinned when it saw her, and although it looked good-natured, it had very long claws and a great many teeth. She felt that it ought to be treated with respect, and she resolved to mind her manners.

“Cheshire Puss,” she began, rather timidly, since she did not know whether it would like the name, but it only grinned a little wider. “Come, it is pleased so far,” thought Alice, and she went on and asked whether it would tell her which way she ought to go from here. The question seemed to her perfectly reasonable, and she waited politely, with her hands folded, for an answer.

“That depends a good deal on where you want to get to,” said the Cat, and Alice replied that she did not much care where, so long as she arrived somewhere. “Then it does not matter which way you go,” said the Cat, adding that she was certain to arrive somewhere if only she walked long enough. Alice felt that this proposition could not be denied, so she abandoned the question of roads and tried another, more practical one.

She asked what sort of people lived about there, and the Cat, waving its right paw round, said that a Hatter lived in that direction, while in that direction, waving the other paw, lived a March Hare. “Visit either one you like,” it said, in the tone of someone recommending two equally excellent restaurants, “they are both mad.” “But I do not want to go among mad people,” Alice remarked, rather alarmed.

“Oh, you cannot help that,” said the Cat, “we are all mad here, I am mad and you are mad.” Alice asked how it knew that she was mad, and the Cat answered that she must be, or she would not have come there. Alice did not think that proved anything, but she went on and asked how it knew that it was mad itself.

“To begin with,” said the Cat, “a dog is not mad, and a dog growls when it is angry and wags its tail when it is pleased.” “Now I growl when I am pleased and wag my tail when I am angry, and therefore I am mad.” “I call it purring, not growling,” said Alice, and the Cat answered that she could call it what she liked.

The Cat asked whether she would play croquet with the Queen that day, and Alice said that she would like it very much but had not yet been invited. “You will see me there,” said the Cat, and vanished, which did not surprise Alice much, since she was getting used to queer things happening. Before long it appeared again to ask what had become of the baby, and when Alice answered that it had turned into a pig, it said that it had thought so, and vanished once more.

Alice waited a little, half expecting to see it again, and sure enough the Cat reappeared, asking whether she had said pig or fig. She answered that she had said pig and begged it not to keep appearing and vanishing so suddenly, because it made her quite giddy. This time the Cat vanished very slowly, beginning with the end of its tail and ending with its grin, which remained in the air for some time after the rest of it had gone.

“Well, I have often seen a cat without a grin,” thought Alice, “but a grin without a cat is the most curious thing I ever saw in all my life.” She walked on a little way, in the direction where the March Hare was said to live, and soon she came in sight of the house. She knew it at once, because the chimneys were shaped like ears and the roof was thatched with fur.

It was such a large house that she did not like to go nearer till she had nibbled more of the left-hand bit of mushroom, and raised herself to about two feet high. Even then she walked up towards it rather timidly, saying to herself that perhaps the March Hare would be raving mad after all, and that she almost wished she had gone to see the Hatter instead. It was not a thought calculated to make her feel any braver, and her steps grew slower as she drew near.

There was a table set out under a tree in front of the house, and the March Hare and the Hatter were drinking tea at it. A Dormouse was sitting fast asleep between them, and the other two were resting their elbows on it as if it were a cushion, talking over its head. Alice thought it must be very uncomfortable for the Dormouse, but since it was asleep, she supposed that it did not mind.

The table was a large one, but the three of them were crowded together at one corner of it, and they cried that there was no room as soon as they saw Alice coming. Alice declared indignantly that there was plenty of room, and she sat down in a large armchair at one end of the table. It seemed to her a very odd way of welcoming a visitor, and she resolved to behave with perfect composure.

“Have some wine,” the March Hare said in an encouraging tone, but Alice looked all round the table and saw nothing on it but tea. She remarked that she could not see any wine, and the Hare replied that there was none, whereupon Alice observed, angrily, that it was hardly civil of him to offer it. The Hare retorted that it was hardly civil of her to sit down without being invited.

The Hatter had been looking at Alice for some time with great curiosity, and his first remark was that her hair wanted cutting. “You should learn not to make personal remarks,” said Alice severely, “it is very rude.” The Hatter opened his eyes wide on hearing this, but all he said was to ask why a raven was like a writing-desk.

Alice was pleased to hear that they had begun asking riddles, and she said that she believed she could guess the answer to this one. The Hatter told her that she should say what she meant, but Alice insisted that she meant what she said, and that the two things were the same. The Hatter cried that it was not the same thing a bit, for one might just as well say that seeing what you eat is the same as eating what you see.

The Hatter was the first to break the silence, and he asked what day of the month it was, having taken his watch from his pocket to look at it uneasily. Alice thought a little and said that it was the fourth, and the Hatter sighed that it was two days wrong. He blamed the butter, which he said had not suited the works, and the Hare meekly replied that it had been the best butter.

Alice had been looking over his shoulder with some curiosity, and she remarked that it was a funny watch, which told the day of the month and not what o'clock it was. The Hatter muttered that there was no reason why it should, and asked whether her watch told her what year it was. She said that it did not, because the year stayed the same for such a long time together, which, the Hatter replied, was just the case with his, and she was dreadfully puzzled by this.

The Hatter asked whether she had guessed the riddle yet, and Alice said that she gave it up and asked what the answer was. The Hatter said that he had not the slightest idea, and the March Hare said the same, so Alice sighed and said that they should not waste time on riddles that had no answers. The Hatter replied that if she knew Time as well as he did, she would not talk about wasting him, for Time was a person.

“I dare say you never even spoke to Time,” said the Hatter, tossing his head contemptuously, and Alice cautiously replied that perhaps not, but she knew she had to beat time when she learned music. “Ah, that accounts for it,” said the Hatter at once, “for he will not stand beating, not for a moment.” If she kept on good terms with Time, he explained, he would do almost anything with the clock, so that, if it were nine in the morning, one whisper would send it round to half-past one, time for dinner.

The Hatter said sadly that he and Time had quarrelled last March, just before the Hare went mad, at the great concert given by the Queen of Hearts. He had been asked to sing a song about a twinkling bat, and he had hardly finished the first verse when the Queen shouted that he was murdering the time and that his head should be taken off. “And ever since that,” the Hatter went on mournfully, “he will not do a thing I ask, and it is always six o'clock.”

The Hatter said that they kept moving round the table whenever the cups were used up, because they never had time to wash them. Alice asked what happened when they came to the beginning again, but the March Hare yawned and interrupted, proposing that they change the subject, as he was tired of this one. He voted that the young lady should tell them a story, but she was alarmed and said that she did not know any.

They both cried that the Dormouse should tell one, and they pinched it on both sides at once, so that it slowly opened its eyes. It declared in a hoarse, feeble voice that it had not been asleep and had heard every word they were saying. Then, in a great hurry, it began a story about three little sisters, called Elsie, Lacie and Tillie, who lived at the bottom of a well.

Alice, who always took a great interest in questions of eating and drinking, asked what the sisters lived on, and the Dormouse, after thinking for a minute or two, said that they lived on treacle. She gently remarked that they could not have done that, because they would have been ill, and the Dormouse agreed, with a gravity that made her want to laugh, that they were very ill indeed. When Alice asked why they lived at the bottom of a well, the March Hare told her very earnestly to take some more tea.

Alice replied that she had had nothing yet and could not take more, and the Hatter said that she meant she could not take less, since it was very easy to take more than nothing. She helped herself to tea and bread and butter, and turned to the Dormouse and repeated her question, and after a minute of thought it said that it was a treacle well. When she protested that there was no such thing, the Hatter and the Hare hissed for her to hush, and the Dormouse sulked.

The Dormouse said that if she could not be civil she had better finish the story herself, but Alice begged humbly that it would go on, promising not to interrupt again. It consented, saying that the sisters were learning to draw, and Alice, forgetting her promise, asked what they drew, and was told that they drew treacle. The Hatter then declared that he wanted a clean cup and that they should all move one place on, so Alice unwillingly took the March Hare's seat, where he had just upset the milk-jug into his plate.

Alice did not wish to offend the Dormouse again, so she began very cautiously by asking where the sisters drew the treacle from. “You can draw water out of a water-well,” said the Hatter, “so I should think you could draw treacle out of a treacle-well, eh, stupid?” Alice said that they were in the well, and the Dormouse answered that of course they were, well in, which so confused her that she let it go on for some time without interrupting.

The Dormouse yawned and rubbed its eyes, for it was getting very sleepy, and said that they drew all manner of things, everything that began with an M, such as mousetraps, the moon, memory and muchness. Alice, who thought it very odd, asked why with an M, and the March Hare asked why not, so she was silent. When she added that she did not think she had ever seen a drawing of a muchness, the Hatter said that then she should not talk.

This piece of rudeness was more than Alice could bear, so she got up in great disgust and walked off. The Dormouse fell asleep instantly, and neither of the others took the slightest notice of her going, though she looked back once or twice, half hoping that they would call her back. The last time she saw them, they were trying to put the Dormouse into the teapot, and she declared that it was the stupidest tea-party she had ever been to in all her life.

Just then she noticed that one of the trees had a door leading right into it, and she thought that was very curious, but that everything was curious today. She decided that she might as well go in at once, and she found herself once more in the long hall, close to the little glass table. She resolved to manage better this time, and her heart beat faster as she looked at the golden key.

She began by taking the little golden key and unlocking the door that led into the garden, and then she nibbled the piece of mushroom she had kept in her pocket, until she was about a foot high. Next she walked down the little passage, and her heart leapt with joy, for the way was open at last. Then she found herself in the beautiful garden, among the bright flower-beds and the cool fountains, and the sunlight lay golden on the grass.

Near the entrance of the garden stood a large rose tree, which bore white roses, but three gardeners were busily engaged in painting them red. Alice thought this very curious, and she went nearer to watch them, taking care not to be seen by any of the three busy painters. As she came up, she heard one of them say that another should look out, and not go splashing paint over him like that, and the quarrel that followed was about who had jogged whose elbow.

One of the gardeners flung down his brush in disgust, but then he saw Alice standing by, and he checked himself, and all of them bowed low. Alice asked timidly why they were painting the roses, and Two explained that this ought to have been a red rose tree, but they had put in a white one by mistake. If the Queen found out, they would all lose their heads, but then Five cried that she was coming, and the three of them threw themselves flat upon their faces.

There was a sound of many footsteps, and Alice looked round, eager to see the Queen. First came ten soldiers carrying clubs, who were shaped like the three gardeners, oblong and flat, with their hands and feet at the corners, and then ten courtiers ornamented all over with diamonds, who walked two and two. After these came the royal children, ten of them, ornamented with hearts, skipping merrily hand in hand, and then the guests, among them the White Rabbit, and last of all the King and Queen of Hearts.

Alice was rather doubtful whether she ought not to lie down on her face like the three gardeners, but she could not remember ever having heard of such a rule at processions. She thought that, besides, there would be no use in a procession if everybody lay down so that they could not see it, so she stood where she was and waited. When the procession came opposite to her, it stopped, and the Queen asked sternly who this was, and then she addressed Alice herself, and Alice told her name very politely, adding privately that they were only a pack of cards.

The Queen pointed to the gardeners lying round the rose tree and asked who they were, for with their faces down she could not tell them from her soldiers and courtiers. Alice answered, surprised at her own courage, that it was no business of hers, and the Queen turned crimson with fury. She glared at Alice like a wild beast and began to scream for her head, but the King laid a hand on her arm and begged her timidly to consider that Alice was only a child.

The Queen turned angrily away from him and told the Knave to turn the gardeners over, and he did so very carefully with one foot, and she screamed at them to get up. They jumped up and began bowing to the King, the Queen, the royal children and everybody else, until the Queen told them to leave off, because they made her giddy. When she saw what they had done to the roses, she cried for their heads to be taken off, and Alice put them into a large flower-pot that stood near, so the soldiers marched off without finding them.

The Queen asked whether their heads were off, and the soldiers shouted in reply that they were gone, if it pleased her Majesty. That was right, said the Queen, and she turned to ask whether Alice could play croquet, but the soldiers were silent and looked at Alice, since the question was evidently meant for her. Alice shouted that she could, whereupon the Queen roared at her to come on, and she joined the procession, wondering very much what would happen next.

A timid voice at her side remarked that it was a very fine day, and Alice saw that she was walking beside the White Rabbit, who was peeping anxiously into her face. She agreed that it was very fine and asked where the Duchess was, and the Rabbit begged her, in a low, hurried tone, to hush. He looked anxiously over his shoulder, raised himself upon tiptoe, put his mouth close to her ear and whispered that the Duchess was under sentence of execution.

Alice asked what the Duchess had done, and the Rabbit asked whether she had said what a pity, but she answered that she thought it no pity at all. The Rabbit began to explain that the Duchess had boxed the Queen's ears, and Alice gave a little scream of laughter. The Rabbit whispered in a frightened tone that she must hush, for the Queen would hear her, since the Duchess had come rather late and the Queen had said something about it.

The Queen shouted at everyone in a voice of thunder to get to their places, and people began running about in all directions, tumbling up against each other. However, they got settled down in a minute or two, and the game began, with a great deal of shouting and confusion on every side. Alice thought she had never seen such a curious croquet-ground in her whole life, and she looked about her in amazement.

Alice thought she had never seen such a curious croquet-ground in her life, for it was all ridges and furrows. The balls were live hedgehogs and the mallets were live flamingos, and the soldiers had to double themselves up and stand on their hands and feet to make the arches. It was a game that no sensible person would have invented, and it was certainly not one whose rules she knew.

The chief difficulty Alice found at first was managing her flamingo, which she tucked comfortably under her arm, with its legs hanging down. Generally, just as she had straightened its neck and was going to strike, it would twist round and look up in her face with such a puzzled expression that she burst out laughing. When she had got its head down again, the hedgehog had unrolled itself and was crawling away, and there was always a ridge or furrow in the way of wherever she wanted it to go.

The players all played at once without waiting for turns, quarrelling all the while and fighting for the hedgehogs, and in a very short time the Queen was in a furious passion. She went stamping about and ordering someone's head off about once in a minute, and Alice began to feel very uneasy. To be sure, she had not yet had any dispute with the Queen, but she knew that it might happen at any moment, and then, she thought, what would become of her?

She was looking about for some way of escape, and wondering whether she could get away without being seen, when she noticed a curious appearance in the air. It puzzled her at first, but after watching it for a minute or two she made it out to be a grin, and she said to herself that it was the Cheshire Cat. When the whole head had appeared, Alice put down her flamingo and began an account of the game, feeling very glad that she had somebody to listen.

She complained that she did not think they played at all fairly, and that they quarrelled so dreadfully one could not hear oneself speak. It was most confusing, she said, to have everything alive, for the next arch was walking about at the other end of the ground. The Cat, who seemed to have been listening with great interest, asked in a low voice how she liked the Queen.

Alice began to say that she did not like her at all, but she noticed just then that the Queen was close behind, listening. So she went on smoothly that the Queen was so likely to win that it was hardly worth while finishing the game, and the Queen smiled and passed on. The King then came up, looked at the Cat's head with great curiosity, and declared that he did not like the look of it at all, though it might kiss his hand if it liked.

The Cat remarked that it would rather not, and the King told it not to be impertinent and not to look at him like that, hiding behind Alice as he spoke. Alice reminded him that a cat may look at a king, having read it in some book, but the King said very decidedly that it must be removed. He called to the Queen, who had only one way of settling difficulties, and she said without even looking round that its head should come off, so the King hurried away to fetch the executioner.

Alice thought she might as well go back and see how the game was going, for she could hear the Queen's voice in the distance, screaming with passion. She had already heard her sentence three players to be executed for missing their turns, and she did not like the look of things at all. So she went in search of her hedgehog, which was fighting with another one, while her flamingo had flown across the garden and was trying helplessly to get up into a tree.

By the time she had caught the flamingo and brought it back, the fight was over and both hedgehogs were out of sight. She tucked the flamingo under her arm, so that it should not escape again, and went back to have a little more conversation with her friend. She was surprised to find quite a large crowd gathered round the Cat, with the executioner, the King and the Queen all talking at once in a dispute, while the rest stood silent and uncomfortable.

The executioner argued that you could not cut off a head unless there was a body to cut it off from, and that he had never done such a thing before. The King argued that anything with a head could be beheaded, while the Queen argued that unless something was done in less than no time, she would have everybody executed all round. Alice could think of nothing to say but that the Cat belonged to the Duchess, so the Queen sent for her, and the Cat's head began fading away the moment the executioner was gone.

The Duchess said how glad she was to see Alice again, the dear old thing, and she tucked her arm affectionately into Alice's, and they walked off together. Alice was very glad to find her in such a pleasant temper, and she thought that perhaps it was only the pepper that had made her so fierce when they met in the kitchen. She told herself that when she was a Duchess, she would not have any pepper in her kitchen at all.

Perhaps it was always pepper that made people hot-tempered, she thought, and vinegar that made them sour, and sweet things that made children sweet-tempered, and she only wished people knew that. She had quite forgotten the Duchess by this time, and was a little startled to hear her voice close to her ear, saying that everything had a moral, if only one could find it. The Duchess squeezed up closer to her side as she spoke, and rested her sharp little chin on Alice's shoulder.

Alice did not much like keeping so close, first because the Duchess was very ugly, and secondly because her chin was uncomfortably sharp, but she did not like to be rude, so she bore it as well as she could. The Duchess said that flamingos and mustard both bit, and that the moral of that was that birds of a feather flock together, and Alice remarked that mustard was not a bird. “Right, as usual,” said the Duchess, “it is a mineral, and there is a large mustard-mine near here.”

The Duchess agreed with everything that Alice said, and found a moral for every remark, even a very long one that Alice said she could not follow unless it was written down. “Pray do not trouble to say it any longer than that,” said Alice, and she thought that it was a cheap sort of present. Then, in the middle of the Duchess's favourite word, her voice died away and her arm began to tremble, and Alice looked up to see the Queen standing in front of them with her arms folded, frowning like a thunderstorm.

“Now, I give you fair warning,” shouted the Queen, stamping on the ground, “either you or your head must be off, and that in about half no time!” The Duchess took her choice and was gone in a moment, and Alice was too frightened to say a word, but slowly followed the Queen back to the croquet-ground. All the while the Queen quarrelled with the other players, and by the end of half an hour every player but the King, the Queen and Alice was in custody, under sentence of execution.

Then the Queen left off, quite out of breath, and asked Alice whether she had seen the Mock Turtle, which she explained was the thing that Mock Turtle soup is made from. Alice said that she had never seen or heard of one, and as they walked off together, she heard the King say softly to the company that they were all pardoned. They soon came upon a Gryphon, fast asleep in the sun, and the Queen ordered it to take the young lady to see the Mock Turtle, and then hurried away to see after her executions.

The Gryphon sat up and rubbed its eyes, then watched the Queen until she was out of sight, and then it chuckled and said what fun it was. It was all her fancy, said the Gryphon, for nobody was ever executed, and it told her to come on, though Alice thought that everybody here ordered her about. Before long they saw the Mock Turtle sitting sad and lonely on a little ledge of rock, sighing as if his heart would break.

Alice pitied him deeply, and asked the Gryphon what his sorrow was, but the Gryphon said that it was all his fancy and that he had no sorrow at all. So they went up to the Mock Turtle, who looked at them with large eyes full of tears but said nothing, and the Gryphon said that this young lady wanted to know his history. “I will tell it her,” said the Mock Turtle, “and nobody is to speak till I have finished,” and after a long silence he sighed that he had once been a real Turtle.

These words were followed by a very long silence, broken only by an occasional exclamation from the Gryphon and the constant heavy sobbing of the Mock Turtle, and Alice very nearly got up and thanked him for his interesting story. At last the Mock Turtle went on, more calmly, that when they were little they went to school in the sea, and the master was an old Turtle, whom they called Tortoise. Alice asked why they called him that, if he was not one, and the Mock Turtle said angrily that they called him Tortoise because he taught us, and that she was very dull.

The Mock Turtle said that they had the best of educations and that they went to school every day, and he asked anxiously whether Alice had extras at hers, like French and music and washing. Alice said that they learned French and music but not washing, and the Mock Turtle said with great relief that then hers was not a really good school. He had only taken the regular course, he said, which began with Reeling and Writhing, and went on to the branches of Arithmetic, Ambition, Distraction, Uglification and Derision.

Alice said that she had never heard of uglification, and the Gryphon lifted both paws in surprise, declaring that she must know what to beautify meant. Alice said doubtfully that it meant to make anything prettier, and the Gryphon said that if she did not know what to uglify was, she was a simpleton. Alice did not feel encouraged to ask more, so she turned to the Mock Turtle, who counted off his other subjects on his flippers, among them Mystery, Seaography and Drawling.

The Drawling-master, the Mock Turtle explained, was an old conger-eel who came once a week, and he said that he could not show Alice what Fainting in Coils was like because he was too stiff. Alice asked how many hours a day they did lessons, and the Mock Turtle said ten hours the first day, nine the next, and so on. “That is the reason they are called lessons,” the Gryphon remarked, “because they lessen from day to day,” and Alice worked out that the eleventh day must have been a holiday.

Alice asked eagerly how they managed on the twelfth day, but the Gryphon interrupted in a very decided tone that that was enough about lessons, and told the Mock Turtle to talk about the games. The Mock Turtle sighed deeply and tried to speak, but sobs choked his voice, and the Gryphon shook him and punched him in the back, as if he had a bone in his throat. When he had recovered, he said with tears running down his cheeks that she could have no idea what a delightful thing a Lobster Quadrille was.

“You first form into a line along the sea-shore,” said the Gryphon, and the Mock Turtle cried that there were two lines, of seals, turtles, salmon and so on, once all the jelly-fish had been cleared out of the way. Then, he said, you advanced twice, each with a lobster as partner, and set to partners, and changed lobsters, and threw them as far out to sea as you could. Both creatures capered wildly about as they explained how you swam after them and turned a somersault in the sea, and then, quite suddenly, they sat down again, very sadly and quietly, and looked at Alice.

“It must be a very pretty dance,” said Alice timidly, and the Mock Turtle asked whether she would like to see a little of it, and said that they could do without lobsters. So they began solemnly dancing round and round Alice, every now and then treading on her toes when they passed too close, and waving their forepaws to mark the time. While they danced, the Mock Turtle sang, very slowly and sadly, a song in which a whiting begs a snail to walk faster, because a porpoise is close behind them.

Alice thanked them, saying that it was a very interesting dance to watch and that she liked the song about the whiting, and the Mock Turtle asked whether she had seen them, of course. She said that she often saw them at dinner, and checked herself, and when pressed she said that they had their tails in their mouths and were all over crumbs. The Mock Turtle said that crumbs would wash off in the sea, and the Gryphon explained that the whitings had been thrown into the sea and got their tails stuck fast in their mouths.

“I can tell you more than that, if you like,” said the Gryphon, and he asked whether she knew why it was called a whiting, and Alice said that she had never thought about it. “It does the boots and shoes,” the Gryphon replied very solemnly, and Alice, thoroughly puzzled, looked down at her own shoes and said that they were done with blacking. “Boots and shoes under the sea,” the Gryphon went on in a deep voice, “are done with a whiting, and they are made of soles and eels, of course.”

Alice, whose thoughts were still running on the song, said that if she had been the whiting she would have told the porpoise to keep back, as they did not want him with them. The Mock Turtle replied that they were obliged to have him, since no wise fish would go anywhere without a porpoise, and when Alice asked whether he meant purpose, he said that he meant what he said. The Gryphon then asked to hear some of her adventures, and she said that she could tell them from that morning, since she was a different person yesterday.

Alice began to tell them her adventures from the time she first saw the White Rabbit, a little nervous at first because the two creatures sat so close and opened their eyes and mouths so wide. They were perfectly quiet until she reached the poem she had recited to the Caterpillar, and when the words came out different, the Mock Turtle drew a long breath and said that was very curious. The Gryphon told her to stand up and recite a verse about the sluggard, and she did, but her head was so full of the Lobster Quadrille that the words came out very queer indeed.

The Gryphon declared that it was different from what he used to say as a child, and the Mock Turtle said that it sounded uncommon nonsense. Alice sat down with her face in her hands, wondering whether anything would ever happen in a natural way again, while the Mock Turtle sang a sad song about beautiful soup. He had scarcely begun the chorus when a cry that the trial was beginning rang out, and the Gryphon hurried Alice away by the hand, while the song about the soup faded behind them.

Alice arrived with the Gryphon at a court where the King and Queen of Hearts were seated on their thrones, with a great crowd assembled about them, and the whole pack of cards stood by. The Knave of Hearts stood before them in chains, with a soldier on each side to guard him, and near the King was the White Rabbit, with a trumpet in one hand and a scroll of parchment in the other. In the very middle of the court stood a table, with a large dish of tarts upon it.

The King was the judge, and he wore his great wig over his crown, which did not look at all comfortable and was certainly not becoming. Alice knew about courts from books she had read, and she was pleased to find that she knew the names of nearly everything there. The jury-box held twelve creatures of various kinds, all writing busily on slates, though Alice could not see what they were writing, since nothing had happened yet.

One of the jurors was Bill the Lizard, whose pencil squeaked, and this Alice could not stand, so she went round the court, got behind him, and very soon found an opportunity of taking it away. She did it so quickly that the poor little Lizard could not make out in the least what had become of it. After hunting about for it, he was obliged to write with one finger for the rest of the day, which was of very little use, as it left no mark on the slate.

The King told the Rabbit to read the accusation, and the Rabbit blew three blasts on the trumpet and then unrolled the parchment scroll. He read in a loud voice that the Queen of Hearts made some tarts, all on a summer day, and that the Knave of Hearts stole those tarts and took them quite away. The King told the jury to consider their verdict, but the Rabbit hastily said that there was a great deal to come before that.

The first witness called was the Hatter, who came in with a teacup in one hand and a piece of bread and butter in the other. He begged pardon for bringing them in, but said that he had not quite finished his tea when he was sent for. The King told him that he ought to have finished, and asked him when he had begun, and the Hatter looked at the March Hare, who had followed him into court arm in arm with the Dormouse.

“Take off your hat,” said the King to the Hatter, who replied that it was not his hat, and the King turned to the jury, who instantly made a note of the fact that the hat was stolen. The Hatter explained that he kept his hats to sell, that he had none of his own, and that he was a hatter. Then the Queen put on her spectacles and began staring hard at him, until he turned pale and fidgeted from one foot to the other.

“Give your evidence,” said the King, “and do not be nervous, or I will have you executed on the spot.” This did not seem to encourage the witness at all, for he kept shifting from one foot to the other, looking uneasily at the Queen. In his confusion he bit a large piece out of his teacup instead of the bread and butter, and just then Alice felt a very curious sensation, which puzzled her until she made out what it was.

She was beginning to grow larger again, and she thought of leaving the court, but on second thoughts she decided to stay where she was as long as there was room. The Hatter said in a trembling voice that he was a poor man and that, what with the thin bread and butter and the twinkling of the tea, he hardly knew where he was. The King asked what the twinkling of what, and the Hatter answered that it began with the tea, and the King snapped that of course twinkling began with a T.

“I wish you would not squeeze so,” said the Dormouse, who was sitting next to Alice, and Alice replied that she could not help it, for she was growing. When the King said that the Hatter might go, he hurried out without his shoes, and the Queen ordered his head cut off outside, but he was out of sight before anyone could try. Meanwhile the next witness, the Duchess's cook, came in carrying the pepper-box, and the people near the door began sneezing all at once.

The King told the Cook to give her evidence, but she refused, and when he asked what tarts were made of, she replied that they were made of pepper, though a sleepy voice said treacle. In an instant the whole court was in confusion, with everybody trying to collar the Dormouse, and when the Cook had vanished, the White Rabbit called the name of the next witness in a shrill little voice. To her great surprise it was Alice, and she jumped up in such a hurry that the edge of her skirt upset the jury-box.

Alice cried out in dismay that she begged their pardon, and she began picking the jurors up as quickly as she could, for the accident of the goldfish kept running in her head. She had a vague idea that they must be collected at once and put back into the jury-box, or they would die, so she scooped them up with both hands and tumbled them into their places. Not a single juror was hurt, though several looked rather ruffled by their adventure and glared at her from their seats.

“The trial cannot proceed,” said the King, in a very grave voice, “until all the jurymen are back in their proper places, all of them,” and he said it looking hard at Alice as he spoke. Alice looked at the jury-box and saw that in her haste she had put the Lizard in head downwards, and the poor little thing was waving its tail about in a melancholy way, being quite unable to move. She soon got it out again and put it right, though she thought that it would not be much use to the trial one way or the other.

As soon as the jury had recovered from the shock of being upset, and their slates and pencils had been handed back, they set to work to write out a history of the accident. All except the Lizard did so, for he seemed too much overcome to do anything but sit with his mouth open, gazing up into the roof of the court. The King then asked Alice what she knew about the business, and she answered that she knew nothing, and when he pressed her whether nothing whatever, she repeated that it was nothing whatever.

“That is very important,” the King said, turning to the jury, but the White Rabbit interrupted in a respectful tone to say that his Majesty meant unimportant, and made faces at him. The King said quickly that he meant unimportant, of course, and he went on muttering to himself, important, unimportant, unimportant, important, as if he were trying out which word sounded best. Some of the jury wrote it down important, and some unimportant, as Alice could see, for she was near enough to look over their slates.

At this moment the King called out for silence and read from his notebook that Rule Forty-two said that all persons more than a mile high must leave the court. Everybody looked at Alice, who protested that she was not a mile high, and the King insisted that she was, and the Queen added that she was nearly two miles high. It was a perfectly absurd accusation, but nobody in that court seemed to doubt it for a moment.

“Well, I will not go, at any rate,” said Alice, “besides, that is not a regular rule, and you invented it just now.” “It is the oldest rule in the book,” said the King, and Alice replied that in that case it ought to be Rule One. The King turned pale and shut his notebook hastily, and he said in a low, trembling voice to the jury that they should consider their verdict, and glanced uneasily at the Queen.

“There is more evidence to come yet, please your Majesty,” said the White Rabbit, jumping up in a great hurry, and he explained that this paper had just been picked up. It seemed to be a letter, written by the prisoner to somebody, and the Rabbit added that there was no direction on the outside and that it was not in the prisoner's handwriting, which was the queerest thing about it. The Knave said that he had not written it, and that nobody could prove that he had, since there was no name signed at the end.

“If you did not sign it,” said the King, “that only makes the matter worse, for you must have meant some mischief, or you would have signed your name like an honest man.” There was general clapping of hands at this, for it was the first really clever thing the King had said that day. “That proves his guilt,” said the Queen, but Alice exclaimed that it proved nothing of the sort, and that they did not even know what the verses were about.

“Read them,” said the King, and the White Rabbit put on his spectacles and asked where he should begin, and the King told him gravely to begin at the beginning and stop at the end. The verses were a strange jumble of he and she and I and they, in which nobody could tell who had given what to whom. When the reading was done, Alice said loudly that she would give a coin to anyone who could explain them, for she did not believe there was an atom of meaning in the whole poem.

The King said that if there was no meaning in it, that saved a world of trouble, and yet he seemed to see some meaning in the verses after all. He spread them out on his knee, looked at them with one eye, and asked the Knave whether he could swim. The Knave shook his head sadly and asked whether he looked like it, which he certainly did not, being made entirely of cardboard.

The King, with growing satisfaction, declared that the verses spoke of the tarts upon the table, and that nothing could be clearer, and he announced that this was the best evidence they had heard yet. The Queen was too furious to hear any more, and she cried that the jury could not yet decide, since the sentence should come first and the verdict afterwards. It was a proposal of such a splendid unfairness that the whole court fell silent.

“Stuff and nonsense,” said Alice loudly, “the very idea of having the sentence first, and the verdict afterwards!” The Queen turned purple with rage and told her to hold her tongue, and when Alice said that she would not, the Queen shouted for her head to be cut off. Nobody moved at all, for they were only a pack of cards, and Alice stared at them in astonishment.

Alice had grown to her full size by this time, and the whole court seemed to her no more than a crowd of painted cards, and not at all alarming. She said, in the clearest voice she could find, that nobody cared for them, as they were nothing but a pack of cards. It was the boldest speech she had made in the whole of her adventure, and a curious silence followed it.

At this the whole pack rose up into the air and came flying down upon her, and Alice gave a little scream, half of fright and half of anger, and tried to beat them off. The cards seemed to whirl about her like autumn leaves, and she thought she would be buried beneath them. She struck out wildly with both arms, and the next moment everything was quiet.

Then she found herself lying on the riverbank, with her head in her sister's lap, while her sister gently brushed away some dead leaves that had fluttered down upon her face. The afternoon was as bright and warm as it had been when she had first grown sleepy, and the river murmured softly in the reeds. It seemed to Alice that she had been away for a very long time indeed.

Her sister told her to wake up, since she had had such a long sleep, and Alice said that she had had such a curious dream. She told her sister, as well as she could remember them, all of her strange adventures, from the White Rabbit to the flying cards. When she had finished, her sister looked at her with a smile that was half amused and half thoughtful.

Her sister kissed her and said that it had certainly been a curious dream, but that now Alice must run in to her tea, since it was getting late. Alice got up and ran off, thinking as she ran, and well she might, what a wonderful dream it had been. The little girl had no idea yet that the dream would stay with her all her life.

Alice jumped up from the grass and ran off across the field with the sunlight on her hair, laughing a little to herself as she went. Every part of the dream was still so clear in her mind that she could hardly believe it had not really happened. She pictured the White Rabbit, the Duchess and the Queen, and she knew that she would never forget a single one of them.

But her sister sat still just as she had left her, leaning her head on her hand, watching the setting sun and thinking of little Alice and all her wonderful adventures, until she too began dreaming after a fashion. In her dream she heard the rattle of the teacups as the March Hare and his friends shared their never-ending meal, and the shrill voice of the Queen ordering off her guests' heads. She heard the baby sneezing on the Duchess's knee, while plates and dishes crashed around it.

She also saw how this same little sister would, in the after-time, become a grown woman, and would keep through her riper years the simple and loving heart of her childhood. She would gather other little children about her and make their eyes bright and eager with many a strange tale, perhaps even the dream of Wonderland of long ago. And she would feel for all their simple sorrows and take pleasure in all their simple joys, remembering her own child-life and the happy summer days.
